create_image_pro_flash.name: create_image_pro_flash
create_image_pro_flash.description:
Create one Pro Flash pixel-art image with an optional left-box style image.

Custom sizes (Beta) accept width and height from 16 to 256 in multiples of 4 pixels.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for native presets and provisional cost.
The style image accepts {url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}; prefer URLs
for uploaded images. Style art must fit the native canvas without resizing.
For several assets of one game, pass the same anchor sprite as style_image on
every call (e.g. the hero's south rotation URL from get_character); without it
each call picks its own look.
style_options selects color_palette, outline, detail and shading independently.
Default style uses existing PixelLab art. For a console or palette look (1-bit,
Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus
`palette_name`: the image is drawn for the palette and every pixel of the result
is one of its colours; the style image keeps lending its look. Returns one image; the provisional
generation charge varies with the canvas. Failed pixel grids use image-to-
pixel-art with fixer on the generated box. Poll get_image(job_id); use
source_image_id after completion.

width.description: Native sizes: 16x16 (experimental), 24x24, 32x32, 32x48, 48x48, 64x64, 96x64, 96x96, 128x128. Custom size (Beta): integer width 16–256 and height 16–256. Both dimensions must be multiples of 4 pixels. Pixel-grid recovery uses image-to-pixel-art with fixer when needed. No native image resizing.

style_image.description: One URL, encoded image, or owned image ID plus its reference instructions.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

style_options.description: Choose which visual traits to copy from the style image.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. The image is drawn for these colours and every pixel of the result is one of them.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours in the image (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

edit_image_pro_flash.name: edit_image_pro_flash
edit_image_pro_flash.description:
Edit one Pro Flash image at its unchanged native canvas size.

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
method=text requires description; method=reference requires reference_image
({url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}). References must fit the source canvas.
No-background defaults to the source's transparency. Optional palette
correction matches source colors. Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for exact
shapes. Returns one queued image; poll get_image(job_id), then download.

reference_image.description: One URL, encoded image, or owned image ID plus its reference instructions.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

inpaint_image.name: inpaint_image
inpaint_image.description:
Regenerate one region of an image, keeping everything else pixel-identical.

This is the repair tool: fix a malformed hand, erase a stray pixel cluster,
swap just the cape, add an item to a specific spot. The area outside the
mask is frozen, so the rest of the sprite cannot drift.

Give the area as a rectangle (easiest — you only need coordinates):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="a clean open hand",
                mask_x=18, mask_y=30, mask_width=14, mask_height=14)
or supply your own mask (white = regenerate, black = keep):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="...", mask_image_base64=<png>)

Related: edit_image rewrites the WHOLE image from an instruction (no mask);
create_map_object generates a new object matching a background's style and
returns a transparent cutout, not your edited image.

Image must be 32x32-512x512; above 256px on a side needs a Tier 2 plan.
Cost: 10 generations for any canvas up to 256x256 (so 64x64 and 88x88 are both
10), 15 up to 341x341, 25 above. The whole image sets the price, not the mask.
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What should appear in the masked area (e.g. 'a clean four-finger hand holding a sword', 'plain grass, no object').

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to repair. 32x32 to 512x512. Everything outside the mask is preserved exactly. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64, which corrupts the image.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the PNG to repair. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite — inline base64 is often cut off mid-string by MCP clients. Give one, not both.

mask_x.description: Left edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_y.description: Top edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_width.description: Width of the area to regenerate.

mask_height.description: Height of the area to regenerate.

mask_image_base64.description: Custom mask, same size as the image: WHITE = regenerate, BLACK = keep. Use instead of mask_x/y/width/height when the area isn't a rectangle.

mask_image_url.description: Alternative to mask_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the mask PNG. Give one, not both.

crop_to_mask.description: Confine generated content to the mask boundary for clean edges.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the input: a sprite with transparency stays transparent, an opaque image stays opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

inpaint_image_pro_flash.name: inpaint_image_pro_flash
inpaint_image_pro_flash.description:
Replace white-mask pixels with Pro Flash, preserving unmasked RGBA bytes exactly.

Source: image_url, image_base64, or owned source_image_id. Mask: a rectangle
(all four mask_x/y/width/height), OR a same-size mask PNG via base64/URL.
Mask RGB must be pure white=generate or black=keep; mask alpha is ignored.
Empty masks are rejected. crop_to_mask is always true. Changes-only output
is transparent outside the mask; Modify current layer returns a composite.
Optional context_image requires bounding_box locating the source and is at
most three times its native dimensions. No images or masks are rescaled.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for shapes; poll the job with get_image.

context_image.description: One URL, encoded image, or owned image ID plus its reference instructions.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

bounding_box.description: The native source rectangle within the additional context image.

create_character_pro_flash.name: create_character_pro_flash
create_character_pro_flash.description:
Create a Pro Flash character from text, including its first image and eight V3 views.

Supply description, optional width/height (default 64x64), and style_image.
For a cast that matches (enemies drawn like the hero), pass the same anchor
sprite as style_image on every call (e.g. the hero's south rotation URL from
get_character); without it each call picks its own look.
Animals: set template_id (bear, cat, dog, horse, lion) and keep 64x64 or larger
(at 48x48 a cat came out small). Say "standing on all four legs" if it will
walk: a cat and a dog came out sitting without it.
Custom sizes (Beta) accept width and height from 16 to 256 in multiples of 4 pixels.
First-direction generation is built in; no separate preview tool is needed.
Alternatively reuse source_image_id or first_frame_url/base64 and omit size
and style settings. A chosen image is preserved with transparent V3 padding,
and only rotations are charged. Never provide both image sources.
Poll get_character(character_id) or the returned outer background job until
completed, including skeleton preparation, before downloading or animating.

width.description: Defaults to 64 for text creation. Native sizes: 16x16 (experimental), 24x24, 32x32, 32x48, 48x48, 64x64, 96x64, 96x96, 128x128. Custom size (Beta): integer width 16–256 and height 16–256. Both dimensions must be multiples of 4 pixels. Pixel-grid recovery uses image-to-pixel-art with fixer when needed. No native image resizing.

style_image.description: One URL, encoded image, or owned image ID plus its reference instructions.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

style_options.description: Choose which visual traits to copy from the style image.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

create_object_pro_flash.name: create_object_pro_flash
create_object_pro_flash.description:
Create a Pro Flash object from text, with one direction or eight V3 views.

Supply description, optional width/height (default 64x64), and style_image.
For props that match a game's characters, pass the same anchor sprite as
style_image on every call (e.g. the hero's south rotation URL from
get_character); without it each call picks its own look.
Custom sizes (Beta) accept width and height from 16 to 256 in multiples of 4 pixels.
First-direction generation is built into this call. n_directions=1 charges
for one new image; n_directions=8 also charges for rotations. Alternatively
reuse source_image_id or first_frame_url/base64 and omit size/style settings:
saving one direction is then free, and eight views charge only rotations.
Objects remain objects without skeletons. Poll get_object(object_id), then
download its PNG (one direction) or ZIP (eight). No preview is regenerated.

width.description: Defaults to 64 for text creation. Native sizes: 16x16 (experimental), 24x24, 32x32, 32x48, 48x48, 64x64, 96x64, 96x96, 128x128. Custom size (Beta): integer width 16–256 and height 16–256. Both dimensions must be multiples of 4 pixels. Pixel-grid recovery uses image-to-pixel-art with fixer when needed. No native image resizing.

get_pro_flash_capabilities.name: get_pro_flash_capabilities
get_pro_flash_capabilities.description:
Get Pro Flash exact native size pairs, controls and one-image output counts.

Free identity-only lookup. Supply operation, width and height together for
a provisional quote split into image/rotations/total. Finishing a selected
preview bills only rotations; one-direction object finalization costs zero.
Larger research sizes are not supported generation sizes. Read this before
selecting dimensions for image, character or object creation, edit or inpaint.

add_to_project.name: add_to_project
add_to_project.description:
Let a game project use a character, object, tileset or map you already own,
or file an asset (gallery images too) into a game or folder on the website.

A game gets the asset in its asset library; one not yet in any folder is
also filed under that game. A folder only groups assets on the website: the
asset moves into it and keeps every game it is in. Characters and objects
move with all their states.

A project's game can only load art that belongs to that project, and until
now the only way to put art there was to create it from inside Game Builder.
Art made anywhere else — this MCP server, the website — was invisible to
every game, so the only route was to generate it a second time and pay for
it again.

A saved VFX effect id (My effects, vfx_workbench export) is not linked:
the reply gives its files (game pack with manifest: frame order, timing,
anchor) as download links and the command that puts them in the game.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

project_id.description: A game or folder project, from list_projects

asset_id.description: A character, object, tileset, map or gallery image you own — the id from list_characters, list_objects, list_topdown_tilesets, list_maps or list_images — or a saved VFX effect id (My effects)

remove_from_project.name: remove_from_project
remove_from_project.description:
Stop a game project from using a character, object, tileset or map.

This unlinks the art from the project. It does NOT delete the art: the
asset stays in your library and can be added back at any time, and any
other project using it is untouched. Use delete_character / delete_object /
delete_topdown_tileset / delete_map to actually destroy something.

Until now add_to_project had no inverse, so a project could accumulate art
it no longer used — and a map that fails to export blocks every deploy of
that project, with no way back out.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

project_id.description: The game project, from list_projects

asset_id.description: A character, object, tileset or map currently in the project — the id you passed to add_to_project

create_character.name: create_character
create_character.description:
Queue character creation. Returns immediately with character ID. Use get_character to check status. It takes NO seed and cannot be made reproducible — unusually for the family, since create_character_pro_flash and create_character_state both do; to keep a look across characters pass style_character_id or a reference image instead.

Which mode: v3 (default) for heroes, enemies and NPCs: clearly more detailed sprites than standard, 2 generations up to 88 px. For a quadruped from text, create_character_pro_flash(template_id=...) at 64 px. Pro when a new character must match an existing one (style_character_id) or to follow concept art. Standard for the lowest cost.
Standard mode: 1 generation, 4 or 8 directions, ~2-5 min. Style params are soft guidance (the model tries to follow them but results may vary).
Pro mode: 10-25 generations, always 8 directions, higher quality. Ignores all style/proportions params. Accepts style_character_id to match an existing 8-direction character's style, and concept_image_url to design the character from concept art, a painting or a photo.
Pro mode only: pass `palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) for a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any Lospec palette): all 8 directions are drawn for it and every pixel is one of its colours.
v3 mode: 2-9 generations, 8 directions, highest quality. Outline and detail are soft guidance; shading/proportions ignored.
v3 + reference_image_base64 / reference_image_url: rotates YOUR south-facing sprite into 8 (or 4) directions — use this (not create_8_direction_object) to turn an existing character sprite into a full character. Works for humanoids and quadrupeds (pass body_type="quadruped" + template). Add direction_images for directions you already drew; v3 fills only the rest.
v3 without a reference image draws the sprite itself and is humanoid only.
Humanoid: bipedal characters with proportion customization.
Quadruped: 4-legged animals — requires template param (bear, cat, dog, horse, lion).

description.description: Character appearance (e.g., 'cute wizard with blue robes'). v3 without a reference draws a two-armed, two-legged figure whatever this says (a slime or a bird comes out humanoid); for an animal see body_type.

name.description: Character name for reference (e.g., 'Blue Wizard', 'Tabby Cat')

body_type.description: Body type. "humanoid" for bipedal characters (people, robots). "quadruped" for 4-legged animals - requires `template` parameter. Available quadruped templates: `bear`, `cat`, `dog`, `horse`, `lion`. Quadrupeds work in mode="standard", mode="pro", and mode="v3" WITH a reference image (south-facing sprite + template); v3 without a reference image is humanoid only (its sprite generator only draws humanoids).

template.description: Quadruped template to use (required when body_type='quadruped'). Available: `bear`, `cat`, `dog`, `horse`, `lion`. Ignored for humanoid body type.

mode.description: Generation mode, default "v3": clearly more detailed sprites than standard, for 2 generations up to 88 px. For a quadruped from text use create_character_pro_flash(template_id=...) at 64 px (6 generations), or mode="pro" or mode="standard" here; v3 draws one only from a reference sprite. "standard" uses template-based skeleton generation (cheaper, 1 generation). "pro" uses AI reference-based generation for higher quality (costs 10-25 generations depending on size, always 8 directions). "v3" produces the highest quality output (costs 2-9 generations depending on size) and is the only mode that accepts reference_image_base64 / reference_image_url (rotate an existing sprite) and direction_images. Pro mode ignores n_directions, outline, shading, detail, text_guidance_scale, and proportions. v3 mode ignores shading, proportions, and text_guidance_scale; v3 honours n_directions only with a reference image (without one it is always 8).

n_directions.description: Number of directional views (4 or 8). Ignored in pro mode and in v3 without a reference image (always 8). With a v3 reference, 4 keeps south/east/north/west.

reference_image_base64.description: South-facing character sprite (PNG base64, max 256x256). Requires mode="v3": rotates this exact sprite into 8 directions — the right tool for turning an existing character sprite into a full rotating character (do NOT use create_8_direction_object for characters). The image defines identity and style; description guides the rotation; outline/detail hints are ignored. SOUTH MEANS STRAIGHT-ON, FACING THE VIEWER: whatever this sprite faces is taken as south and every other direction is rotated from it, so a 3/4 turn here silently offsets the WHOLE set by 45 degrees and every direction label is wrong. There is no way to declare a different facing — re-pose or pick a front-on reference first, or you pay for eight unusable sprites. Output size defaults to the reference's own dimensions unless size is set. PREFER reference_image_url for anything above ~32x32 — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

style_character_id.description: ID of one of your existing 8-direction characters to use as the style reference (mode="pro" only). Its 8 directional sprites guide the new character's style in every direction. The style character must be completed with 8 directions, and size must be at least its sprite content size — the job fails fast with the required size otherwise.

reference_image_url.description: Alternative to reference_image_base64: an https URL to the south-facing sprite PNG (mode="v3" only). South means STRAIGHT-ON, facing the viewer: whatever this sprite faces becomes south and the other seven are rotated from it, so a 3/4-turn reference offsets every direction and mislabels the whole set. PREFER THIS for anything but tiny sprites — inline base64 is often cut off mid-string by MCP clients, which corrupts the image. Give a url OR a base64, not both.

concept_image_url.description: mode="pro" only: concept art, a painting, sketch or photo of the character (any pose or angle; larger than 1024 px is scaled down to fit) that the 8 directions are designed from. The result keeps its look, not its pose or canvas. An https or data: URL. For a finished sprite you want rotated as drawn, use mode="v3" with reference_image_url instead.

concept_image_base64.description: Alternative to concept_image_url: the concept as PNG/JPEG base64. Give a url OR a base64, not both.

direction_images.description: Requires mode="v3" and a reference image: sprites you already drew for OTHER directions, as {direction: image}. Directions: south-east, east, north-east, north, north-west, west, south-west (with n_directions=4 only east, north, west). Each image is an https URL, upload:<id>, data URL, or PNG base64, like the reference. They are used exactly as drawn and v3 generates only the directions you leave out; cover every one and nothing is generated (import, 0.25 generations). Every image must have the same canvas size as the reference and face the direction it is keyed under. If your client cannot send an object here, send the same object JSON-encoded as a string.

proportions.description: Character body proportions as JSON string (humanoid only, ignored for quadrupeds). PRESET: Use built-in proportions like '{"type": "preset", "name": "chibi"}' (options: default, chibi, cartoon, stylized, realistic_male, realistic_female, heroic). CUSTOM: Define exact values like '{"type": "custom", "head_size": 1.5, "arms_length": 0.8, "legs_length": 0.9, "shoulder_width": 0.7, "hip_width": 0.8}' (all values 0.5-2.0)

size.description: Character size in pixels (default 48). Max 128 for standard/pro mode; up to 256 for mode="v3". Standard mode treats this as the size of the character and stores it on a canvas ~40% larger (64 -> 92x92, 128 -> 180x180) so animations fit. Pro mode stores rotations on a shared square canvas at least this large. V3 from scratch sends this as the requested square generation size; with a v3 reference image, omitted size uses the reference dimensions and a supplied size is advisory.

outline.description: Outline style hint (soft guidance — the model may not follow exactly). Ignored in pro mode.

shading.description: Shading hint (soft guidance — the model may not follow exactly). Ignored in pro and v3 modes.

detail.description: Detail level hint (soft guidance — the model may not follow exactly). Ignored in pro mode.

text_guidance_scale.description: How closely to follow the text description (higher=more faithful). Default 8.0.

view.description: Camera angle. "low top-down" (~20° from above, classic 3/4 RPG), "high top-down" (~35° steeper angle), "side" (eye-level), "oblique" (BETA: 3/4 oblique projection, max 128px, 4-dir only, standard mode only).

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

create_character_state.name: create_character_state
create_character_state.description:
Queue a state (variant) of an existing character. The new character keeps
the source's identity, body type, and proportions, with the edit applied
consistently across all 4 or 8 rotations. Auto-waits up to 30s for the
source to complete.

A character is a group of states: `name` is the character's name (shared by
all states), and each state has its own `state_name` — defaulting to the
edit description truncated to 20 characters (a new character's first state
is named "Idle"). Pass `state_name` to name the new state explicitly.

IMPORTANT — this ALWAYS preserves the SAME individual's face and identity,
even for edits like "elderly", "wounded", or a different class/role. It makes
a variant OF this character (different outfit/pose/state), NOT a new character.
To make a DIFFERENT character in the same art style, use create_character with
matching size/view/outline/shading/detail params (and a v3 reference image if
you want to match the look) — not create_character_state.

Returns a new character_id grouped with the source via group_id. Inspect
sibling states with `get_character` on either id.

`palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) puts every direction of the state on
those colours, the source's rotations first; it can't be combined with
use_color_palette_from_reference (max_colors alone can).

Cost: 10-25 generations — the tier is resolved from the canvas at generation
time, so the exact charge is not known when the call is made. The balance
check runs against the 10 floor, which means a call CAN charge more than it
reserved. Leave 25 generations of headroom, or check get_balance first, if
you are near the end of a plan.

Generation time: ~1-5 minutes (async). Poll with get_character(character_id).

character_id.description: Source character UUID to create a state of

edit_description.description: Edit instructions describing the new state (e.g. 'sitting down', 'wearing red armor', 'fighting pose').

state_name.description: Name for the new state (e.g. 'Sitting', 'Red Armor'). Defaults to the edit description truncated to 20 characters.

use_color_palette_from_reference.description: Snap the edited rotations to the source character's existing color palette so the new state stays color-consistent with the original. Do not enable when the edit is meant to introduce new colors.

override_width.description: Optional larger canvas WIDTH for the state — reach for it when the edit adds something big (a weapon, wings) needing room beyond the character's tight canvas. Multiple of 4, no smaller than the source width. Pair with override_height; omit both to keep the source size.

override_height.description: Optional larger canvas HEIGHT for the state (see override_width). Multiple of 4, no smaller than the source height.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

animate_character.name: animate_character
animate_character.description:
Queue animation for a character. Returns immediately with job IDs. ~2-4 min.

Modes (auto-detected, override with `mode`):
- template: provide template_animation_id. 1 gen/direction; canvases over ~100px run in batches billed 1 each (256px: 4-9/direction, 30+ min) — the receipt gives the ceiling. Frame count fixed by template.
- v3 (default when no template): custom from action_description. Cost is ceil(w·h·frames/65536) per direction on the GENERATED canvas, not the sprite — the silhouette grows it, so a 96px character commonly animates at ~132px and bills 3 rather than 2, and the frames are STORED at that canvas (a 128px character's come back ~176-180px; there is no keep-native-size option). At 8 frames before growth: 64px=1/dir, 96px and 128px=2, 160px=4, 256px=8. Directions are summed, not multiplied: each sizes its own canvas. frame_count 4-16.
- pixminimax (beta): custom from action_description on PixMiniMax. frame_count multiples of 4 up to 40 at any size. Priced by canvas and frame count (64x64 at 4/8/16/40 frames = 1/1/2/6 gen/direction); the response's cost line is what was charged. ~1-7 min/direction.
- skeleton-v3 (beta): the template_animation_id clip posed onto the character, steadier identity. 2-4 gen/direction.

Animates all character directions by default (v3/pixminimax default to south only).
Use get_character to see available template animations.

Custom keyframes (mode='v3' or 'pixminimax', single direction): pass
custom_start_frame_base64 to override the starting pose, and/or
end_frame_base64 to interpolate toward a target pose.

Quality escalation (try next if result is poor — delete_animation first, then retry):
1. template (1 gen/dir) — standard walk/run/idle
2. v3 (2/dir at 96px before the silhouette grows the canvas, ~4/dir at 160px) — custom action_description, cheap re-roll for small sprites
3. pixminimax (1-6/dir) — custom action_description, longer clips, cheap at large sizes

Cost: template mode bills 1 generation per direction up to a ~92px canvas.
Above that the clip splits into batches billed 1 each, so the charge follows
the CLIP's frame count as well as the canvas: at 128px breathing-idle (4
frames) bills 1 per direction and walking (6 frames) bills 2; at 180px, 2 and
3; at 256px it is one generation per frame — 4 and 6 — and a direction takes
30+ min. The longest clips set the worst case: jumping-1 (9 frames) bills 3 at
128px, 5 at 180px, 9 at 256px. Frame counts are fixed by the clip and run 1 to
17 (static is 1, lead-jab 3, breathing-idle 4, walk/walking/cross-punch 6,
any `-N-frames` clip is N); get_character lists your character's clips, and
the submit receipt gives the exact ceiling before anything runs.
v3: ceil(w*h*frames/65536) per direction on the GENERATED canvas.
pixminimax: 64x64 at 4/8/16/40 frames = 1/1/2/6 per direction.
skeleton-v3: 2-4 per direction.

template_animation_id.description: Template animation ID. Required for template-based animations (1 generation/direction). Omit for custom animations that use action_description instead — defaults to v3 mode. v3 cost is ceil(canvas²·frames/65536) per direction on the GENERATED canvas, which the silhouette grows past the sprite size: at 8 frames 64px=1/dir, 96px and 128px=2/dir, 160px=4/dir, 256px=8/dir BEFORE that growth, and a 96px character commonly animates at ~132px and bills 3. Read the cost line in the response for what was actually charged. Asked for a humanoid action by NAME, map it to a real id rather than inferring one: hurt/recoil/stagger/hit -> `taking-punch`, death/downed/dying -> `falling-back-death` then `getting-up`, dash/dodge/sprint -> `running-slide` or `running-jump`, cast/spell/magic -> `fireball`. `hurt`, `dashing`, `casting`, `backstep-dodge`, `shooting` and `staff-spin-attack` do NOT exist and are refused before the job is queued. The COMPLETE humanoid set, each id with its frame count in brackets: `backflip` (10), `breathing-idle` (4), `cross-punch` (6), `crouched-walking` (6), `crouching` (5), `drinking` (6), `falling-back-death` (7), `fight-stance-idle-8-frames` (8), `fireball` (6), `flying-kick` (6), `front-flip` (6), `getting-up` (5), `high-kick` (7), `hurricane-kick` (4), `jumping-1` (9), `jumping-2` (8), `lead-jab` (3), `leg-sweep` (7), `picking-up` (5), `pull-heavy-object` (6), `pushing` (6), `roundhouse-kick` (7), `running-4-frames` (4), `running-6-frames` (6), `running-8-frames` (8), `running-jump` (8), `running-slide` (6), `sad-walk` (8), `scary-walk` (8), `surprise-uppercut` (7), `taking-punch` (6), `throw-object` (7), `two-footed-jump` (7), `walk` (6), `walk-1` (6), `walk-2` (6), `walking` (6), `walking-10` (6), `walking-2` (4), `walking-3` (6), `walking-4` (6), `walking-4-frames` (4), `walking-5` (4), `walking-6` (6), `walking-6-frames` (6), `walking-7` (6), `walking-8` (6), `walking-8-frames` (8), `walking-9` (6). Template mode returns exactly that many frames and has no frame-count override. skeleton-v3 prices off the same count — 3 frames is 2 generations/direction, 4-14 is 3, 15 is 4 — so every clip here bills 3 except `lead-jab`. Quadruped animations vary by template - use get_character() to see available animations.

action_description.description: Custom action description focusing on the movement or pose only (e.g., 'walking stealthily', 'walking quickly', 'running', 'jumping', 'casting spell'). Avoid environmental details like locations or objects. If not provided, uses default for template_animation_id.

animation_name.description: Custom name for this animation, stored as display_name. If you are appending to an existing animation_group_id, PASS THE GROUP'S EXISTING NAME — it is NOT inherited. Omitting it leaves the new directions with no display_name, so get_character falls back to the animation type and the group looks renamed (e.g. a group called 'delver_cape_walk' starts showing as 'walking-8-frames').

animation_group_id.description: Append these directions to an EXISTING animation group instead of starting a new one. Pass the [group: ...] id shown by get_character(). Use this to fill in missing directions of an animation you already started (e.g. a rate-limited call that only landed 5/8 directions) so they stay one group. Pass animation_name too, repeating the group's existing name — it is not inherited, and omitting it makes the group appear renamed. Omit animation_group_id to mint a fresh group. Must belong to this character.

directions.description: Specific directions to animate (e.g., ['south', 'east']). Valid values: south, north, east, west, south-east, south-west, north-east, north-west. If not provided: template mode animates all character directions, custom mode animates south only.

ai_freedom.description: AI freedom (0-900). TEMPLATE MODE ONLY — ignored in v3 and pixminimax modes. Higher values let the AI deviate more from the template skeleton pose. 0 = rigid template following.

mode.description: Custom-animation engine. "template": skeleton from template_animation_id (1 gen/direction; canvases over ~100px run in batches billed 1 each, the receipt gives the ceiling). "skeleton-v3": the SAME template_animation_id posed onto the character, which moves the character instead of redrawing it each frame — steadier identity and colours, 2-4 generations and ~3-5 min per direction, beta. "v3" (default when no template_animation_id): custom animation from action_description with frame_count control, cheap, one job per direction. "pixminimax": custom animation from action_description on PixMiniMax (beta, every tier) — longer clips (multiples of 4 up to 40 frames) at any size, priced by size and frame count (64x64: 8 frames = 1 gen/direction, 40 frames = 6), ~1-7 min per direction, one job per direction. Auto-detected: template if template_animation_id is given, else v3.

frame_count.description: Number of animation frames. v3 mode: 4-16, even, and canvas width x height x frames may not exceed 8 x 256 x 256 — a 256px canvas takes 8 frames at most, 16 frames fit up to ~180px. pixminimax mode: a multiple of 4 from 4 to 40. In 'template' mode the template's own frame count is used.

custom_start_frame_base64.description:
Optional custom starting pose for the animation (mode='v3' or 'pixminimax'). When omitted, the character's rotation image for the chosen direction is used as the start. Max 256x256.

REQUIRES A SINGLE DIRECTION. Pass directions=[<one cardinal>] (one of: south, south-west, west, north-west, north, north-east, east, south-east), or omit directions to default to south. If the user has not said which direction the animation is for, ask them — do not pick one arbitrarily.

Not compatible with mode='template' or mode='skeleton-v3'.

end_frame_base64.description:
Optional target pose to interpolate toward (mode='v3' or 'pixminimax'). Providing this enables interpolation mode: the model animates between the start frame (rotation image or custom_start_frame_base64) and this end frame. Dimensions must match the start frame.

REQUIRES A SINGLE DIRECTION (see custom_start_frame_base64). Not compatible with mode='template' or mode='skeleton-v3'.

custom_start_frame_url.description: Alternative to custom_start_frame_base64: an https URL to the start-frame PNG (mode='v3' or 'pixminimax'). PREFER THIS for large images — inline base64 is often truncated by MCP clients (cut off mid-string), which corrupts the image. A URL avoids that. Give a url OR a base64, not both, for the same frame.

end_frame_url.description: Alternative to end_frame_base64: an https URL to the end-frame PNG (mode='v3' or 'pixminimax'). PREFER THIS for large images to avoid inline-base64 truncation. Give a url OR a base64, not both, for the same frame.

keep_first_frame.description: Keep the reference frame as frame 0 of the stored animation (mode='v3' or 'pixminimax'). Set false to store exactly frame_count generated frames — the reference start frame is stripped, so frame_count=8 stores 8 frames instead of 9. Not compatible with mode='template' or mode='skeleton-v3'.

subject_description.description: mode='pixminimax' only: what the character is, one noun phrase (e.g. 'a knight in silver plate armour'). Omit to have it read from the character's image; fill it in if a job fails saying our AI declined.

initial_pose.description: mode='pixminimax' only: the pose the first frame is in (e.g. 'standing upright with the sword lowered'). Omit to have it read from the image.

create_topdown_tileset.name: create_topdown_tileset
create_topdown_tileset.description:
Generate a Wang tileset for top-down game maps with corner-based autotiling.

This tool starts an asynchronous tileset generation that returns immediately with a tileset ID.
Use get_topdown_tileset to check status and retrieve the completed tileset.

Which mode: standard (default) is the website's standard tileset, cheap and
fast. mode="pro" paints the richest tiles (textured ground, raised banks, more
shape controls): use it when the look matters, standard when cost does.

Cost: standard is 1 generation now that it runs on pixen. (The classic model
it replaced billed per stage: 1-4, usually 3 or 4 — NOT 1, over 6,124 prod
charges, mean 3.1.) mode="pro" costs 15 generations for tiles up to 32 px,
25 above. Failed jobs are not charged.

Tile count depends on mode and transition depth:
  - standard mode: 0.0 through 0.5   → 16 tiles (4x4);  >0.5 → 25 tiles (4x8)
  - pro mode:      0.0 / 0.25       → 16 tiles;        0.5 / 1.0 → 25 tiles
(pro promotes 0.5 past the 0.4 threshold, so a pro request at 0.5 returns 25,
not 16.) The 25-tile layout has 21 distinct corner combos — the 4 extra
wall-continuation tiles share corners with a twin and are distinguished by
pattern_4x4, not corners.
Vertices define terrain, tiles render based on their 4 corner values.

Pro border shape (mode="pro"): roundness (0 square, 1 round, 2 corners cut at
45 degrees), boundary_amplitude + boundary_seed (a meandering border instead of
a straight one; tall walls get a gentler one), step_slope (a raised bank from a
cliff at 0 to a gentle slope at 2; transition_size 0.25), connect_diagonals
(the two diagonal tiles' upper corners joined into one area). A value the
chosen set can't draw is refused with what to send instead.

Use case: Building top-down game maps with seamless terrain transitions.

Algorithm: For each grid cell, sample terrain at 4 vertices, select matching tile.

## Creating Connected Tilesets

One tileset holds exactly two terrains. Three or more (e.g. grass, dirt and
water) need a chain of tilesets sharing a terrain, or the terrains that never
share a set have no tiles to meet. Use base tile IDs to connect them:

1. Create first tileset (e.g., ocean→beach) and wait for completion
2. Use get_topdown_tileset to retrieve the base tile IDs
3. Use the beach base tile ID as lower_base_tile_id for next tileset (beach→grass)

Example workflow:
- Tileset 1: ocean (lower) → beach (upper) → get beach base tile ID
- Tileset 2: beach (lower, using base tile ID) → grass (upper) → get grass base tile ID
- Tileset 3: grass (lower, using base tile ID) → stone (upper)

This ensures visual consistency across terrain transitions.

mode="pro" takes a palette (its hex colours, e.g. Game Boy or PICO-8, plus
palette_name): the set is drawn for those colours and every pixel of every tile
is one of them, except connected terrain, which stays as the other tileset made it.

Generation time: standard ~30 seconds, pro a few minutes (async processing)

transition_size.description: How far the upper terrain rises above the lower: 0 = flat, 1.0 = full-tile walls. Standard takes any value from 0 to 1 (above 0.5 = 25 tiles, 16 px tiles only); pro uses the nearest of 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 (0.5 and up = 25 tiles).

transition_description.description: The strip between the terrains, e.g. 'wet sand with foam'. Used only when transition_size > 0; at the default 0 there is no strip to draw.

tile_size.description: Tile dimensions as {"width": N, "height": N}, OR a bare int N for a square tile (same shape create_tiles_pro accepts). 16 or 32 for standard; 64 requires mode='pro'.

mode.description: Generation pipeline. "standard": the website's standard tileset (pixen, 16 or 32px, round borders unless shape_style='square'), cheap and fast. "pro": the richest tiles - painted texture, raised banks - 16/32/64px; use it when the look matters. raggedness, roundness, boundary_amplitude and step_slope shape its border (not shape_style - mode='pro' with shape_style is rejected); connects through lower_base_tile_id/upper_base_tile_id like standard.

shape_style.description: Terrain-boundary geometry for mode='standard' (passing it with mode='pro' is rejected). 'round' (default for standard, as on the website) for circular arcs, 'square' for stepped corners. transition_size is continuous from 0 to 1; values above 0.5 use a 4x8 sheet.

enhance.description: Standard tilesets only (on by default; pro ignores it). AI-enhances the terrain descriptions at the chosen detail/shading levels and picks matching base colours before generation. The stored tileset keeps the enhanced text; your original prompts are kept in its metadata.

spread_x.description: No effect - the Pro pipeline no longer uses it; kept so existing calls work.

slope_size.description: No effect - the Pro pipeline no longer uses it; kept so existing calls work.

raggedness.description: Pro only. Terrain boundary noise (0=smooth, 1=rough). Tall sets (transition_size above 0.4) are half as rough.

roundness.description: mode='pro' or shape_style only. Corner shape of the border between the two terrains: 0 = square, 1 = round, 2 = corners cut at 45 degrees (values in between blend). Above 1 needs mode='pro'. Omit for the default (0.85 on pro, 0.6 with shape_style). On tall pro sets (transition_size above 0.4) up to 1 leaves the corners to the shape picked from the descriptions, and 1-2 cuts them toward 45 degrees.

boundary_amplitude.description: Uneven boundary: mode='pro' (any transition_size), or shape_style with transition_size up to 0.5. How far the border between the terrains meanders instead of running straight, 0 = straight (default) to 0.3 = the most. Tiles still connect seamlessly. On a raised pro set a taller bank gets a gentler curve (half at transition_size 0.25), and tall walls (above 0.4) gentler still.

boundary_seed.description: Boundary shape for boundary_amplitude: another number gives a different meander at the same amount; the same number gives the same shape.

step_slope.description: Edge steepness: mode='pro' with transition_size 0.25 only (a raised 16-tile set). How the bank between the terrains falls: 0 = a cliff, straight down (default), up to 2.0 = a gentle slope spread over more ground.

connect_diagonals.description: mode='pro' only. The two diagonal tiles (upper terrain in opposite corners): true joins the two upper corners through the middle into one area; false (default) leaves the lower terrain running between them. On tall walls (transition_size above 0.4) the upper corner's wall turns forward to meet the lower block.

outline.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

view.description: Camera angle, mode='pro' only: match your characters' view (create_character defaults to low top-down). Standard (pixen) always draws high top-down.

tile_strength.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

lower_base_tile_id.description: ID of existing tile to use as lower terrain reference. Use to create connected tilesets

upper_base_tile_id.description: ID of existing tile to use as upper terrain reference. Use to create connected tilesets

tileset_adherence.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

tileset_adherence_freedom.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

text_guidance_scale.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

create_sidescroller_tileset.name: create_sidescroller_tileset
create_sidescroller_tileset.description:
Generate a sidescroller tileset for 2D platformer games with side-view perspective.

This tool starts an asynchronous tileset generation that returns immediately with a tileset ID.
Use get_sidescroller_tileset to check status and retrieve the completed tileset.

Which mode: standard (default) is the website's standard sidescroller tileset
(pixen, side view), cheap and fast. mode="pro" paints the richest platforms;
use it when the look matters, standard when cost does.

Cost: standard is 1 generation now that it runs on pixen. (The classic model
it replaced billed 2 or 3 generations — NOT 1, over 1,186 prod charges, mean
2.6.) mode="pro" costs 15 generations for 16 or 32 px tiles. Failed jobs are
not charged.

Creates tilesets optimized for 2D platformer games:
- Side-view perspective (not top-down)
- Transparent background (no background terrain)
- Platform/ground tiles with flat surfaces (no slopes)
- Optional decorative transition layer on top of base terrain

Use case: Building 2D platformer games with seamless terrain tiles.

## Creating Connected Tilesets

Use base tile IDs to create multiple tilesets that seamlessly connect:

1. Create first tileset (e.g., stone platform, either mode) and wait for completion
2. Use get_sidescroller_tileset to retrieve the base tile ID
3. Pass that base tile ID with mode="pro" to create the next tileset

Chaining needs mode="pro": standard draws the new top around every edge of a
chained platform instead of only on top.

The base tile is the platform body: chaining reuses it and draws a new top.
Example workflow:
- Tileset 1: stone brick platform, grass on top → get base tile ID
- Tileset 2: stone brick platform, snow on top (stone base tile ID, mode="pro")
- Tileset 3: stone brick platform, moss on top (same base tile ID, mode="pro")

A different body (wood, metal) is a new tileset without base_tile_id.

Generation time: standard ~30 seconds, pro a few minutes (async processing)

transition_size.description: Size of terrain transition. Controls how much of the surface layer appears (0.0 = no surface layer, 0.25 = light surface layer, 0.5 = heavy surface layer). Snapped to the nearest of 0, 0.25 and 0.5.

mode.description: "standard": the website's standard sidescroller tileset (pixen, side view), cheap and fast. "pro": the richest platforms - painted texture, a cleaner cap - use it when the look matters.

enhance.description: mode='standard' only. AI-enhances the platform and surface descriptions and picks matching base colours before generation. The stored tileset keeps the enhanced text; your original prompts are kept in its metadata.

tile_size.description: Tile dimensions as {"width": N, "height": N}, OR a bare int N for a square tile (same shape create_tiles_pro accepts). 16 or 32 pixels.

outline.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

tile_strength.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

base_tile_id.description: mode='pro' only. base_tile_id from get_sidescroller_tileset: the platform body is reused, so describe the same body in lower_description and the new top in transition_description

tileset_adherence.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

tileset_adherence_freedom.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

text_guidance_scale.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

create_map_object.name: create_map_object
create_map_object.description:
Create a pixel art object with transparent background. ~30-90s. Returns object ID immediately.

Two modes:
- Basic (no background_image): standalone object from description. Requires width/height.
- Style matching (with background_image): matches your map's art style. Width/height auto-detected.
  Default inpainting: oval 60%. Options: oval, rectangle, or custom mask.

Canvas: 32-400px. Basic max 400x400, inpainting max 192x192.
Transparency: the background is transparent up to 40,000px area (200x200, e.g.
128x256, 192x192); larger basic-mode canvases get a flat single-colour one.
background_image: {"type": "base64", "base64": "..."} (file paths not supported)
inpainting: {"type": "oval", "fraction": 0.3} | {"type": "rectangle", "fraction": 0.5} | {"type": "mask", "mask_image": "base64..."}

Use get_map_object to check status. The object is permanent and can be
placed on a map with place_map_object.

width.description: Canvas width in pixels (required for basic mode, auto-detected from background_image if provided)

height.description: Canvas height in pixels (required for basic mode, auto-detected from background_image if provided)

background_image.description: Background image for style matching (optional). Format: {"type": "base64", "base64": "..."}. File paths are not supported (server cannot read local files). If provided without inpainting config, uses default: oval 60%.

inpainting.description: Inpainting configuration as JSON string (optional). DEFAULT: If background_image provided but this omitted, uses oval 0.6. Options: {"type": "oval", "fraction": 0.3} for auto oval mask, {"type": "rectangle", "fraction": 0.5} for auto rectangle mask, {"type": "mask", "mask_image": "base64..."} for custom mask. Mask convention: WHITE (255) = area where AI generates, BLACK (0) = frozen/preserved context. Fraction is 0.05-0.95 (how much of background the shape covers).

get_map_object.name: get_map_object
get_map_object.description:
Get map object status and data. Returns image if completed.
The object is permanent — place it on a map with place_map_object.
Retries saving finished pixels when B2 or database persistence failed.

create_1_direction_object.name: create_1_direction_object
create_1_direction_object.description:
Queue a 1-direction object (10-25 generations, ~30-90s). Returns object_id immediately.

When size ≤170, produces multiple candidates (4/16/64) in 'review' status.
Call get_object to view candidates as inline images, then:
- select_object_frames(object_id, indices=[...]) to keep specific ones
- dismiss_review(object_id) to discard all
Single candidates are kept automatically.

For a fixed palette (Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette`
as its hex colours: objects are drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

size.description: Square image size in pixels (min 16, max 256). Defaults to 64 when omitted. Cannot be set together with style_images — when style_images are provided, the largest style image determines the output size. The effective size also determines how many candidate objects are produced in one shot (≤42→64, ≤85→16, ≤170→4, else 1). Multi-object results enter 'review' status — call get_object to inspect, then select_object_frames or dismiss_review to finalize.

name.description: Object name for reference (e.g., 'wooden barrel', 'Forest Mushroom'). Defaults to the description when omitted.

view.description: View. NOTE: 1-direction uses top-down/sidescroller; create_8_direction_object and create_map_object use a different set (low top-down / high top-down / side).

style_images.description: Style reference images, PNG/JPEG base64 (max 256x256 px each). Each image: {"base64": "<png-data>", "format": "png"}. The maximum count depends on `size`: ≤85 → 8, ≤170 → 4, else → 1. When empty, a default style is used based on `view`. Note: this is NOT the same as reference_image on tileset tools (which is a small 16x16/32x32 texture).

item_descriptions.description: Per-object descriptions when `size` produces multiple objects. Length must not exceed the object count derived from `size`. Supplying FEWER is allowed and does NOT shrink the grid: the remaining slots are generated from `description`, so they come back as extra objects in the same style, not as variations of the items you listed. One description at size=48 therefore returns 16 objects, only the first of which is the one you named.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

create_8_direction_object.name: create_8_direction_object
create_8_direction_object.description:
Queue an 8-direction object rendered from 8 angles (10-25 generations, ~2-4 min).
Returns object_id immediately. Use get_object to check status.
For single-direction objects, use create_1_direction_object instead.
For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any Lospec palette) pass
`palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: all 8 directions are drawn for
it and every pixel is one of its colours.

size.description: Square image size in pixels (min 24, max 168 — below 24 the eight angles stop being distinguishable, so use create_1_direction_object for 16px). Defaults to 64 when omitted. Cannot be set together with reference_image_base64 or style_image_base64 — in those cases the image dimensions determine the output size.

name.description: Object name for reference (e.g., 'Treasure Chest', 'Oak Barrel'). Defaults to the description when omitted.

reference_image_base64.description: Reference image of an OBJECT/item — generates 8 rotations from it. Works well for props (barrels, chests). NOTE: identity transfer is unreliable for CHARACTER/humanoid sprites — the reference sits in the center of a grid of placeholder characters and can lose the salience contest, so the output may resemble a generic character instead. For a character sprite, use create_character(mode="v3", reference_image_base64=...) instead — that pipeline reproduces the input faithfully. Mutually exclusive with style_image_base64.

style_image_base64.description: Style reference — generates a new object matching the description with the style of this image. Mutually exclusive with reference_image_base64.

style_object_id.description: ID of one of your existing 8-direction objects to use as the style reference. Its 8 directional sprites guide the new object's style in every direction. The style object must be completed with 8 directions, and size must be at least its sprite content size — the job fails fast with the required size otherwise.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

get_object.name: get_object
get_object.description:
Get object details. Branches by status:
- processing: progress + ETA
- review: candidate frame URLs + inline previews
- completed: rotation URLs, animations, download link
- failed: error + retry hint

include_preview.description: Embed preview image (south for 8-dir, candidates for review).

list_objects.name: list_objects
list_objects.description:
List your objects with status and progress. One line per object.
Use get_object(object_id) for full details.

tags.description: Comma-separated tags to filter by (matches ANY tag).

status_filter.description: Filter by status: completed, review, pending, processing, failed.

search.description: Filter by name, case-insensitive. Matches the name shown here and the description it was created from, so 'chest' finds 'treasure chest'.

animate_object.name: animate_object
animate_object.description:
Add an animation to an existing object. Returns one queued job per direction
submitted; each job takes ~30-60s.

Cost warning: when generating on a subscription, mode='pro' costs 10-25
generations per direction (80-200 for a full 8-direction animation).
Prefer mode='v3' (default) — it usually produces higher quality results
and is cheaper.

For 1-direction objects, this animates the "unknown" direction. For
8-direction objects, a single call animates all 8 directions of one
animation by default. Pass `directions` to animate a subset, or
`animation_group_id` (from get_object) to add directions to an animation
you've already started.

Interpolation mode (mode='v3' only): pass `end_frame_base64` to interpolate
toward a target pose — the model animates between the start frame and the
end frame. The start defaults to the object's idle frame for that
direction, but you can override it with `custom_start_frame_base64`. When
either frame is provided, exactly one direction must be specified.

Palette (mode='pro' only): pass `palette` as hex colours plus `palette_name`
for a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, Lospec); every pixel
of every direction is one of them.

object_id.description: Object UUID to animate (must be a completed object).

mode.description:
Which animation mode to use. Prefer 'v3' (default) — it usually produces higher quality results than 'pro', and is cheaper. Use 'pro' only when its different stylistic output is specifically needed.

Cost warning: when generating on a subscription, 'pro' mode costs 10-25 generations per direction (80-200 for a full 8-direction animation).

animation_description.description: Describe the animation, e.g. 'walking cheerfully'. Required when creating a new animation; can be omitted when adding directions to an existing animation via animation_group_id (the existing description is inherited).

directions.description:
Which directions to animate.
- Do NOT pass `directions` for 1-direction objects. They always animate the single internal direction; passing this returns an error.
- For 8-direction objects, omit `directions` to animate all 8 cardinals on a new animation, or — when extending an existing animation via `animation_group_id` — to fill in only the cardinals not yet generated. You usually don't need to compute the missing set yourself; passing `animation_group_id` alone is enough. If you do pass `directions` explicitly, it must be a subset of the cardinals.

frame_count.description:
Frames per direction. Independent per-direction — you do NOT need to match the frame_count of existing directions when extending an animation. Just omit this and use the per-mode default.

- mode='v3': any even number 4-16 (default 8). Note: v3 stores the input reference frame alongside the generated ones (unless keep_first_frame=false), so frame_count=8 stores 9 frames total (and that's what get_object reports). To extend a v3 animation that get_object shows as frame_count=9, just omit this field — the default produces a matching 9-frame output.
- mode='pro' depends on object canvas (longest side):
  - canvas ≤ 64px → 16 frames (only)
  - canvas ≤ 128px → 4, 9, or 16 frames
  - canvas ≤ 170px → 9 frames (only)
  - canvas larger than 170px → pro not supported (use mode='v3')
  - default: smallest available count for the canvas size

animation_group_id.description: Mostly only relevant for 8-direction objects: pass the animation_group_id of an existing animation (from get_object) to add more directions to it. Omit to create a new animation; the new animation_group_id is returned so subsequent calls can extend it.

display_name.description: Optional name for the animation, shown in the UI and used when exporting.

replace_existing.description: Set true to regenerate a direction that has already been animated in this animation. Without this, re-animating the same direction returns an error.

confirm_cost.description: Only for pro animations (mode="pro"). NEVER set to true on first call. First call without it to see the cost, then show the cost to the user. Only set to true after the user explicitly confirms they want to spend the generations. Not needed for v3 animations.

custom_start_frame_base64.description:
Optional custom starting pose for the animation (mode='v3' only). When omitted, the object's idle frame for the chosen direction is used as the start. When provided, the image's dimensions become the canvas for the animation (subject to v3's 256x256 maximum).

REQUIRES EXACTLY ONE DIRECTION.
- 8-direction objects: ASK the user which direction the animation should be for before calling this tool. Do NOT pick a direction yourself, and do NOT default to south. The eight options are: south, south-west, west, north-west, north, north-east, east, south-east. Pass the user's choice as directions=[<that direction>].
- 1-direction objects: do not pass `directions` at all; the single internal direction is auto-resolved.

Not compatible with mode='pro'.

end_frame_base64.description: Target pose to interpolate toward (mode='v3' only). The model animates between the start frame (idle or custom_start_frame_base64) and this end frame. Dimensions must match the start frame. Same single-direction requirement as custom_start_frame_base64. Not compatible with mode='pro'.

keep_first_frame.description: Keep the input reference frame as frame 0 of the stored animation (mode='v3' only). Set false to store exactly frame_count generated frames — the reference start frame is stripped, so frame_count=8 stores 8 frames instead of 9. Not compatible with mode='pro'.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

create_object_state.name: create_object_state
create_object_state.description:
Queue a state (variant) of an existing object. Auto-waits up to 30s for the
source object to complete. Returns a new object ID grouped with the source
via group_id.

An object is a group of states: `name` is the object's name (shared by all
states), and each state has its own `state_name` — defaulting to the edit
description truncated to 20 characters (a new object's first state is named
"base"). Pass `state_name` to name the new state explicitly.

A state is the SAME object in another condition (open/closed, lit, broken).
A different item belongs in its own object — for a matching look, pass the
source's image as style_images to create_1_direction_object. States move
together: adding or removing one in a project or folder moves every state.

`palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) puts the state, every direction of
it, on those colours; the source goes on them before the edit.

object_id.description: Source object UUID to create a state of

state_name.description: Name for the new state (e.g. 'Mossy', 'Golden'). Defaults to the edit description truncated to 20 characters.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

delete_object.name: delete_object
delete_object.description:
Permanently delete an object, its rotations/frames, animations, tags,
project assignments, and storage files. Immediate — this cannot be undone.

update_object_tags.name: update_object_tags
update_object_tags.description:
Replace ALL tags on an object (set operation, free, synchronous).

Tags organize and filter objects — see list_objects(tags=...). Passing an
empty list clears every tag. This replaces the full set: include existing
tags you want to keep.

object_id.description: Object UUID whose tags to replace

tags.description: Full replacement tag list (max 20 tags, 50 chars each; whitespace trimmed, case-insensitive dedup). Empty list clears all tags.

select_object_frames.name: select_object_frames
select_object_frames.description:
Promote selected frames of a review object to individual completed objects.

See get_object on a review-status object to view candidates inline.
Each selected index becomes its own 1-direction object. Once no frames
remain in the review object it is deleted automatically. If a call times
out it may still finish: check get_object before retrying (promoted frames
leave the review object, and re-selecting one is refused).

indices.description: 0-based indices of frames to keep. Each becomes a separate completed 1-direction object.

common_tag.description: Optional tag applied to every newly-created object.

dismiss_review.name: dismiss_review
dismiss_review.description:
Discard a review-status object and delete all its candidate frames.
Used when none of the consistent-style candidates are worth keeping.

create_ui_asset.name: create_ui_asset
create_ui_asset.description:
Queue a pixel-art UI panel (10-25 generations, ~30-90s). Returns ui_asset_id immediately.
Omit `pieces` for a default rounded-rect panel. Use get_ui_asset to check status.
For a fixed palette (Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as
its hex colours: the panel is drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

description.description: Style of the UI panel (e.g. 'wooden RPG panel with gold trim')

width.description: Output width in px (192–688). Max is aspect-gated, NOT freely combinable: square ≤512×512, 16:9 ≤688×384, 9:16 ≤384×688, 4:3 ≤600×448, 3:4 ≤448×600. E.g. 688×512 is rejected (resolves to 4:3, max 600×448) — use 688×384 or 512×512.

height.description: Output height in px (192–688). Max is aspect-gated (see width): the two axis maxes cannot be combined — 688 only with a 16:9/9:16 partner (688×384 or 384×688), 512 only as a square (512×512).

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

style_image_base64.description: Optional style reference image (base64 PNG/JPEG, ideally <=1024px per side). The panel matches its palette, pixel scale, outlines and shading — the strongest way to make UI fit an existing game. Only the art style is copied, never its content or layout.

name.description: Friendly name for the saved asset

project_id.description: Optional PixelLab project ID to assign the finished UI asset to

elements.description: Named UI element types to scaffold the panel from (auto-positioned, no coords needed). Available: button, icon_button, toolbar, tab, panel, window, health_bar, avatar, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon. Combine with `pieces` for custom shapes; omit both for a default panel.

pieces.description: Advanced shape template (validated). Each piece needs a unique `id`, a `kind`, and an optional `label`. Allowed kinds: rounded_rect {x,y,w,h,radius}, circle {x,y,r}, polygon {x,y,r,sides,phase}. Coords are on a virtual editor canvas — longer side 0–512, shorter side scaled to the output aspect (a 16:9 panel uses a 512×288 coordinate grid, not the output size). Omit for a default full-canvas panel.

anyOf.description:
Regular polygon — `sides` vertices at distance `r` from (x, y),
starting from angle `phase` (radians).

get_ui_asset.name: get_ui_asset
get_ui_asset.description: Get UI panel details. Processing → progress; completed → image URL + download.

list_ui_assets.name: list_ui_assets
list_ui_assets.description:
List your UI panels with status. One line per asset.
Use get_ui_asset(ui_asset_id) for full details.

delete_ui_asset.name: delete_ui_asset
delete_ui_asset.description:
Permanently delete a UI panel (and, for a template, its split elements + their
states) plus the backing image files. Immediate — this cannot be undone.

search_help.name: search_help
search_help.description:
Ask for help using PixelLab MCP tools, workflows, or features.
A knowledge agent searches our docs and returns a concise answer.

question.description: What you need help with (tools, workflows, billing, features, deployment). Include the context you are working in. Max 2000 characters.

agent_feedback.name: agent_feedback
agent_feedback.description:
Report something broken, confusing or missing — a PixelLab tool, the sandbox
(build, deploy, git, playtest), the game template code, or the website.
Specific beats polite. Read daily by the team.

tool_name.description: What it's about: a tool, command or file (e.g. 'create_character', 'wrangler deploy', 'src/scenes/Game.ts').

message.description: What you did, what happened, what you expected. Be specific.

area.description: Rough bucket, helps route it: generation (art tools), chat_tool, template (the game template's code), sandbox (build, deploy, git, playtest), website, other.

create_tiles_pro.name: create_tiles_pro
create_tiles_pro.description:
Create pixel art tiles (pro).

Generates multiple tile variations by drawing tile shape outlines and having
AI fill them with pixel art. Supports hexagonal, isometric, and square
top-down tile types.

This tool starts asynchronous generation that returns immediately with a tile ID.
Use get_tiles_pro to check status and retrieve completed tiles.

**Two modes:**

1. **Shape mode** (default): Specify tile_type, tile_size, tile_view to control tile shape.
2. **Style mode**: Provide style_images to match existing tiles' style and dimensions.

**Prompting tip:** Number each tile for best control:
"1). grass tile 2). dirt tile 3). stone tile 4). water tile"
One call makes at most 16 independent tiles, fewer at large tile sizes
(get_tiles_pro shows how many); numbered items past that are not drawn.
tile_feature='tileset' makes its own fixed set instead.

Examples:
- "1). grass tile 2). dirt tile 3). stone tile 4). water tile 5). sand tile 6). lava tile"
- "1). ocean water 2). shallow water 3). wet sand 4). dry sand"

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec)
pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: the tiles are drawn for
them and every pixel of every tile is one of them (with style_images the style
tiles' colours are then not copied).

Generation time: ~15-30 seconds (async processing)

description.description: Text description of the tiles. For best control, number each tile: '1). grass tile 2). stone tile 3). lava tile'. At most 16 independent tiles per call: split a longer list.

tile_type.description: Shape of the tiles. hex: flat-top hexagonal, hex_pointy: pointy-top hexagonal, isometric: diamond/rhombus, oblique: true square top with the depth extruded diagonally down-right at 45 degrees (tile_feature='tileset' or 'building' only), octagon: 8-sided polygon, square_topdown: square at angle.

tile_size.description: Tile size in pixels (16-128). 32px is recommended for most use cases.

tile_height.description: Tile height in pixels for non-square tiles (e.g., 128 for 64x128). Omit to compute from tile_type geometry and view angle. Maps (create_map, Map Workshop) take groups made without tile_height, or with tile_size or 2x it. A flat 2:1 iso floor still goes on a map: omit tile_height, set tile_view_angle=30 and tile_depth_ratio=0.

tile_view.description: View angle controlling tile depth. top-down: no depth, high top-down: ~15%, low top-down: ~30%, side: ~50%.

tile_view_angle.description: Continuous view angle in degrees (0-90). Overrides tile_view when provided. 0=side, 90=top-down.

tile_depth_ratio.description: Tile depth/thickness ratio (0.0-1.0). Controls vertical depth. Overrides default from tile_view.

tile_flat_top_px.description: Isometric top/bottom cap width: 2px classic or 4px modern. Only used when tile_type='isometric'.

style_images.description: Style reference tiles as JSON array. When provided, tiles match the style and dimensions of these references. Shape controls (tile_type, tile_size, tile_view, etc.) are ignored. Each entry is {"image": "<reference>"} — an https URL, upload:<id>, gallery:<id>, job:<id>[:<index>] or a pixel tool result id; the size is read from the image, and a reference avoids inline base64 being cut off by the client — or inline {"base64": "...", "width": 64, "height": 80}.

style_options.description: Options for what to copy from style images, as JSON. Format: {"color_palette": true, "outline": true, "detail": true, "shading": true}

outline_mode.description: Tile outline mode. "outline" = gray shading with outlines (default). "segmentation" = RED/BLUE color zones without outlines — produces cleaner tiles with no outline artifacts.

tile_feature.description: Set to "tileset" to generate a connectable TERRAIN TRANSITION instead of independent tiles: a 16-tile corner set for isometric/square_topdown/oblique, or a 32-tile coastline for hex/hex_pointy. Describe it as a transition ("grass to water") — the first terrain is the main one. Returns per-tile placement rules (see get_tiles_pro). Cannot be combined with style_images. For square top-down transitions, create_topdown_tileset is the dedicated tileset model and adds transition width, per-terrain reference images and style matching. For paths use create_path_tiles; for walls/floors use create_building_kit.

oblique_lean.description: Oblique tilesets only: horizontal shear per pixel of depth. 0.5 = classic cabinet (~27 degrees), 1.0 = a full 45 degree diagonal (default).

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

create_path_tiles.name: create_path_tiles
create_path_tiles.description:
Create a connectable PATH/ROAD tile set (18 configs).

Generates straights, corners, T-junctions, a crossroads, dead-ends and a
plain ground tile, all sharing one look. The set ships per-tile edge rules
(N/E/S/W bitmasks), so a map editor or your own autotiler can pick the right
piece from a cell's painted neighbours — see get_tiles_pro for the rules.

For terrain transitions (grass meeting water) use
create_tiles_pro(tile_feature="tileset"); for walls and floors use
create_building_kit.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec)
pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: the set is drawn for them
and every pixel of every tile is one of them.

Non-blocking: returns a tile id immediately; poll with get_tiles_pro.

description.description: Ground and path, e.g. "grass with a dirt road" or "stone floor with a mosaic walkway". Describe both — the set renders the path over the ground.

tile_type.description: Tile shape. square_topdown: square tiles at an angle. isometric: diamond/rhombus.

tile_size.description: Tile size in pixels. square_topdown requires exactly 32; isometric accepts 48-96.

tile_depth_ratio.description: Tile thickness as a fraction of tile size.

outline_mode.description: "outline" = gray shading with outlines. "segmentation" = color zones, cleaner seamless edges.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

create_building_kit.name: create_building_kit
create_building_kit.description:
Create a BUILDING KIT — floor, connectable walls, doorways, pillar, stairs.

Generates a matched vocabulary of architectural pieces (walls 1-3 tiles
high) you assemble into structures. Wall segments carry outline rules so a
cell's walls follow the shape of the floor area you place them around.

Roofs: the kit has two. The upper-floor tile (floor_roof, floor2's material)
is FLAT — lay it on top of the walls for a flat roof, terrace or upper
storey. The roof pieces (materials layout only) slope up from every eave
(`roof_profile`) and flatten inside. A description such as "flat roof"
changes the material only, never this shape.

Not a terrain set: for grass-meets-water use
create_tiles_pro(tile_feature="tileset"); for roads use create_path_tiles.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec)
pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: the kit is drawn for them
and every pixel of every piece is one of them.

Non-blocking: returns a tile id immediately; poll with get_tiles_pro.

wall_description.description: Wall material, e.g. "stone brick walls" or "weathered timber walls".

floor_description.description: Floor material, e.g. "wooden plank floor" or "flagstone floor".

tile_type.description: Projection. isometric: diamond lattice. square_topdown: plain square grid. oblique: true square top with walls sheared down-right at 45 degrees.

tile_size.description: Tile size in pixels. isometric requires 32-96; square_topdown and oblique accept 16-96.

floor2_description.description: Upper-storey / roof surface material: paints the flat upper-floor tile (floor_roof) and the roof pieces. Defaults to the wall material. It sets the material only, not the roof's shape — see roof_profile.

roof_profile.description: Shape of the roof pieces' edges (materials layout only): gable = straight slope, round = curved. Each edge rises over half a tile and the roof is flat inside, so only a one-tile-wide roof peaks. There is no flat roof piece; for a flat roof or a roof terrace, lay the upper-floor tile (floor_roof) on top of the walls. Default gable.

layout.description: grid: each shaped piece is painted individually (richer; isometric default). materials: flat swatches are painted and pieces rendered from them (more consistent; default for square_topdown/oblique).

wall_angle.description: square_topdown only: wall storey height as its own camera angle, decoupled from the ground pitch.

oblique_lean.description: Wall shear per pixel of height. 0.5 = classic cabinet (~27 degrees), 1.0 = a full 45 degree diagonal.
