outline_mode.description: "outline" = gray shading with outlines. "segmentation" = color zones, cleaner seamless edges.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

get_tiles_pro.name: get_tiles_pro
get_tiles_pro.description: Get tiles pro by ID. Returns tile data and storage URLs if completed, or progress if processing.

tile_id.description: The UUID of the tiles pro to retrieve. Each returned tile carries the placement rule its sheet uses; the bit meanings are edge/4: bit0=N bit1=E bit2=S bit3=W; a set bit means the painted feature continues across that edge; edge/6: 6 hex edges CCW from vertex 0; a set bit means the OTHER terrain (water) lies beyond that edge; corner/4: NW<<3 | NE<<2 | SW<<1 | SE; a set bit means the first terrain occupies that corner.

list_tiles_pro.name: list_tiles_pro
list_tiles_pro.description:
List your tiles (pro). One line per tile with status.
Use get_tiles_pro(tile_id) for full details.

limit.description: Maximum number of tiles to return

delete_tiles_pro.name: delete_tiles_pro
delete_tiles_pro.description:
Delete tiles pro by ID. Only the owner can delete their own tiles.

This action is permanent and cannot be undone.

tile_id.description: The UUID of the tiles pro to delete

create_portrait_character.name: create_portrait_character
create_portrait_character.description:
Convert between a portrait and a character sprite (pro).

Preserves the subject's identity/outfit while matching an internal
size-specific pixel-art style for the chosen view. For a fixed palette
(Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours:
the sprite is drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

This tool starts asynchronous generation that returns immediately with a job
ID. Use get_portrait_character to check status and retrieve the sprite.

Examples:
- Turn a character portrait into a top-down RPG sprite:
  create_portrait_character(image_url=<portrait_png_url>, direction="portrait_to_character", view="low top-down", result_size=64)
- Turn a full-body sprite into a bust portrait:
  create_portrait_character(image_url=<character_png_url>, direction="character_to_portrait", view="low top-down", result_size=64)

Generation time: ~30-80 seconds (async processing)

image.description: Input image as base64-encoded PNG. PREFER image_url because MCP/LLM clients can alter or truncate opaque base64 tool arguments.

image_url.description: Public HTTPS URL or data URL for the input image. Prefer this over image so the original bytes do not pass through the model.

direction.description: portrait_to_character: portrait in → full-body character sprite out. character_to_portrait: character in → bust portrait out.

view.description: Camera angle. low top-down: classic 3/4 RPG. high top-down: steeper. side: eye-level sidescroller.

result_size.description: Output sprite size in pixels. Cost: 16/32/48/64 = 10 generations; 128/160 are drawn with extra detail = 15 generations.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

get_portrait_character.name: get_portrait_character
get_portrait_character.description:
Get a portrait ↔ character result by job id.

Returns the sprite (inline + download URL) if completed, or progress/error.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_portrait_character.

set_character_portrait.name: set_character_portrait
set_character_portrait.description:
Attach a bust portrait to a character (no generation, free).

A portrait is the starting frame for talking animations — set one, then
create_vocal_animation generates the mouth positions from it. Overwrites any
existing portrait.

Examples:
- Straight from a portrait job:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", from_job_id="<portrait-job-uuid>")
- From your own artwork:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", image=<png_base64>)

character_id.description: Character to attach the portrait to.

image.description: Portrait as base64-encoded PNG. Square is ideal; a non-square image is centred on a transparent square canvas.

from_job_id.description: Instead of `image`: the job id of a completed create_portrait_character run. The sprite is copied straight across, so it never has to pass through your context.

create_vocal_animation.name: create_vocal_animation
create_vocal_animation.description:
Generate a talking mouth-position set ("visemes") for a character's portrait.

Produces one keyframe per mouth shape, all sharing the chosen expression, so
the character can be lip-synced to any line of text afterwards. Building the
set costs generations ONCE; turning it into talking animations with
create_talking_gif is free.

Works two ways. With `character_id` the set is saved onto that character, so
every later call needs only the id — use this when the character exists.
With `image` you generate straight from a portrait and nothing is stored; the
frames live in the job for 8 hours and you reference it by job id.

Requires a paid plan (tier 1+). The character form needs a portrait set first.

Examples:
- Default talking set for a character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>")
- Add an angry expression to the same character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>", mood="angry")
- Just a portrait, no character:
  create_vocal_animation(image=<portrait_png>)

Generation time: ~2-5 minutes (async processing)

character_id.description: Character to generate the expression for; it must already have a portrait, and the finished set is saved onto it so later calls only need the character id. Mutually exclusive with `image`.

image.description: Generate from this portrait PNG (base64) instead, without a character. Nothing is stored: the mouth positions come back from get_vocal_animation and you pass that job id to create_talking_gif. Use this when the user only has a portrait. Mutually exclusive with `character_id`. Max 256x256.

mood.description: Expression baked into the face (brows/eyes/cheeks). The mouth shapes are the same across moods. One call per mood; each is stored as its own row of the character's vocal grid.

viseme_count.description: How many mouth positions to generate. 3 = minimal (tiny portraits), 5 = basic, 7 = recommended, 12 = high quality (large close-ups). Must match across moods for the same character.

no_background.description: Cut out the background so frames are transparent PNGs — usually what you want for compositing over a game scene.

get_vocal_animation.name: get_vocal_animation
get_vocal_animation.description:
Check a vocal-animation job and see which mouth positions have landed.

Mouth positions stream in as they are picked, so a running job already
reports partial progress. On completion the set is saved onto the character
and ready for create_talking_gif.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_vocal_animation.

create_talking_gif.name: create_talking_gif
create_talking_gif.description:
Turn text into a talking GIF using a character's existing mouth positions.

FREE — no generations are spent. This only sequences frames that
create_vocal_animation already produced, so the expensive step happens once
per expression and every line of dialogue after that costs nothing.

Examples:
- create_talking_gif(character_id="<uuid>", text_to_speak="Welcome, traveller!")
- create_talking_gif(character_id="<uuid>", text_to_speak="You dare return?!", mood="angry")
- portrait-only, no character:
  create_talking_gif(from_job_id="<vocal job id>", text_to_speak="Hello!")

Returns immediately (no job to poll).

text_to_speak.description: The line of dialogue to lip-sync. Mouth shapes are derived from the letters, so any language using the latin alphabet works.

character_id.description: Character with a vocal animation. Mutually exclusive with `from_job_id`.

from_job_id.description: Use a portrait-only set instead: the job id from create_vocal_animation(image=...). Mutually exclusive with `character_id`. Available for 8 hours after that job finished.

mood.description: Which generated expression to talk with. Defaults to the character's first available expression.

frame_ms.description: Milliseconds per mouth position (~90ms reads as natural speech; raise it for a slower delivery). GIF stores delays in 10ms steps, so this is rounded to the nearest 10 and the response reports what was actually used.

hold_ms.description: Pause on the closed mouth at the end so a looping GIF has a beat between takes.

get_lip_sync.name: get_lip_sync
get_lip_sync.description:
Get the lip-sync frame plan for a line of dialogue — for animating in a game.

FREE, and nothing is rendered. Use this instead of create_talking_gif when the
game should animate the mouth itself: you get the spritesheet URL, the row for
the expression, and a frame list giving the column to draw and how long to hold
it. create_talking_gif is the better answer when you just want a playable file.

Timings are exact here — unlike a GIF, an engine can hold a frame for any
duration.

Example:
- get_lip_sync("<uuid>", "Welcome to the village, traveller!")

Returns immediately (no job to poll).

character_id.description: Character with a vocal animation (see create_vocal_animation). This tool is character-only on purpose: it hands the engine a spritesheet URL to load, and a portrait-only set has no stored spritesheet — for that case use create_talking_gif(from_job_id=...) instead.

text_to_speak.description: The line of dialogue to lip-sync.

mood.description: Which generated expression to use. Defaults to the character's first available expression.

frame_ms.description: Milliseconds to hold each mouth position.

hold_ms.description: Extra time on the final closed mouth.

create_font.name: create_font
create_font.description:
Create a pixel-art font (pro).

Produces a glyph atlas + a ready-to-use TrueType (.ttf) font with uppercase,
lowercase, digits 0-9, and common game-UI punctuation. Costs 15 generations
or at least $0.115 in credits.

This tool starts asynchronous generation that returns immediately with a job
ID. Use get_font to check status and retrieve the atlas + font.

Example:
  create_font(description="warm orange arcade font", weight="Bold", glyph_px=16)

Generation time: ~30-80 seconds (async processing)

description.description: Style description of the font, e.g. 'warm orange arcade font'.

glyph_px.description: Native glyph resolution in pixels (real bitmap size per glyph). The atlas is a 10x8 grid of 80 glyphs, ROW-MAJOR, so cell i holds the i-th character of "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz.,!?:;'"-+()0123456789/%*=_$" — slice it with that order. There is no space glyph.

font_name.description: Explicit font family name; defaults to '{description} {weight}'.

get_font.name: get_font
get_font.description:
Get a font result by job id.

Returns the glyph atlas (inline) + download URLs for the atlas PNG and the
.ttf if completed, or progress/error otherwise.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_font.

create_image_pixflux.name: create_image_pixflux
create_image_pixflux.description:
Generate a freeform pixel-art image from text (no character/object rig).

Use this for anything that is just an image: item icons, backgrounds, card
art, props, concept frames. For a rotatable character use create_character;
for an asset-pack prop use create_1_direction_object; for a map prop that
matches an existing map's style use create_map_object.

Canvas is 16-400px per side, total area 32x32 to 400x400.

Examples:
- create_image_pixflux(description="health potion bottle", width=64, height=64, no_background=True)
- create_image_pixflux(description="forest background", width=320, height=180)
- img2img over your own sprite:
  create_image_pixflux(description="same knight but in gold armor", init_image_base64=<png>, init_image_strength=150)

init_image_strength is how much of the input is KEPT (inverted vs most
img2img APIs): 500 barely moves it, 300 is subtle, ~150 is a visible edit,
~50 keeps only the rough composition. For editing an image use edit_image;
for fixing one region use inpaint_image.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'cute dragon', 'health potion bottle').

width.description: Canvas width in pixels. Defaults to the init_image width, or 128 when there is no init_image. The 16px floor is per-axis: the TOTAL area must still be at least 32x32=1024px, so 16x16 is rejected while 16x64 is fine.

height.description: Canvas height in pixels. Defaults to the init_image height, or 128 when there is no init_image. See width for the area rule.

no_background.description: Return the subject on a transparent background. Use True for sprites/items, False for scenes and backgrounds. Unset with an init_image follows that image; unset without one means False.

direction.description: Which way the subject faces (weakly guiding).

text_guidance_scale.description: How literally to follow the description. Higher = more literal.

init_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to start from (img2img). Must be exactly width x height — omit width/height to adopt its size.

init_image_url.description: Alternative to init_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the init PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

init_image_strength.description: How much of init_image is PRESERVED — the opposite of the usual img2img 'strength'. Higher = closer to the input: 500 barely changes it, 300 is subtle, 150 (default) is a real edit, ~50 keeps only the composition.

color_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG whose colors become a forced palette. Any size — only its colors are read.

color_image_url.description: Alternative to color_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the palette PNG. Give one, not both.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

create_image_pixen.name: create_image_pixen
create_image_pixen.description:
Generate a freeform pixel-art image with the Pixen model.

Pixen is the newer of the two fast generators and holds up better on small
sprites. Pick between the three text-to-image tools like this:
- create_image_pixflux — when you need an init image (img2img), a palette
  given as an image, isometric, or shading control.
- create_image_pixen — this one; cleaner small sprites, bigger canvas.
- create_image_pro — best quality, returns a set of candidates, costs more;
  takes a palette as hex colours (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, NES, Lospec).

Canvas: 16-768 per side and each side must be a multiple of 4; total area
16x16 to 512x512. Below 32 the canvas must be SQUARE, so the small sizes
are 16x16, 20x20, 24x24 and 28x28.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'ornate iron key', 'mossy stone wall').

width.description: Canvas width in pixels. Must be a multiple of 4; width must equal height when either side is below 32. width x height may not exceed 512x512 = 262,144, so the widest canvases are e.g. 768x340 or 680x384, not 768x384.

height.description: Canvas height in pixels. Must be a multiple of 4; height must equal width when either side is below 32.

no_background.description: Return the subject on a transparent background. True for sprites and items, False for scenes. Up to 256x256 of area (65,536 px, e.g. 256x256 or 512x128); larger canvases are refused with it on.

direction.description: Which way the subject faces (weakly guiding).

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

create_image_pro.name: create_image_pro
create_image_pro.description:
Generate pixel art with the Pro model — best quality, several candidates.

This is "Create Image (Pro)". It returns a SET of options in one call rather
than a single image, by the larger side: 64 candidates up to 32px, 49 at
33-35px, 36 at 36-41px, 25 at 42-50px, 16 at 51-64px, 9 at 65-84px, 16 at
85px, 4 at 86-170px, 1 above that. Cost is per call, not per candidate, so a
small canvas is where it pays off.

Unlike the other two text-to-image tools it accepts labelled references:
  create_image_pro(
      description="knight in the same armour",
      reference_images='[{"base64": "<hero png>", "usage": "character base"},
                         {"base64": "<armour png>", "usage": "outfit"}]')

No facing control: nothing here sets which way the subject looks, and a
reference does not either. To turn a picture you already have into 8
facings, use create_object_pro_flash(first_frame_base64=..., n_directions=8).

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, NES, any palette from
Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856",
"#88c070", "#e0f8d0"], plus `palette_name`: the image is drawn for the
palette and comes back using only those colours. A palette name alone is not
enough - the colours are what the result is put on. `max_colors` caps the
colours in each image (e.g. 6 for an NES-style sprite).

Pick between the three: create_image_pixflux for img2img or isometric;
create_image_pixen for clean small sprites at 1 generation; this one when
quality matters more than cost, or for a palette given as hex colours.

Cost: 10-25 generations for the CALL, never multiplied by the candidate count.
The rule is one step: the sheet is your canvas times the candidates per side,
and you pay that sheet's tier. Square canvases work out to 10 for 16-32, 43-64,
86-128 and 171-256; 15 for 33-42, 65-85, 129-170 and 257-341; 25 above.
Candidates per call, square canvases by side: 64 for 16-33, 49 for 34-35, 36
for 36-41, 25 for 42-51, 16 for 52-65, 9 for 66-85, 4 for 86-171, 1 from 172.
A NON-SQUARE canvas is not the longest side applied to those ladders, and it is
not the area either: both sides are read, and a narrower canvas can fit one more
per side and so land a tier cheaper. 48x72 returns 16 candidates at 10
generations while 72x72 returns 9 at 15, on the same longest side. Verified
non-square costs: 320x180 and 72x56 are 10, 384x216 and 416x176 are 15, 512x288
and 688x384 are 25. For a size not listed, don't extrapolate from the square
ladders — the submit receipt reports the actual cost and candidate count before
anything renders.
Generation time: ~1-10 minutes (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'ornate iron key with a ruby inlay').

width.description: Canvas width. The cap is an AREA of roughly a quarter megapixel, shaped by whichever of ten aspect ratios your request is nearest to — so no single number is the maximum width. Those maxima: 1:1 512x512, 5:4 576x464, 4:3 600x448, 3:2 632x424, 16:9 688x384, 21:9 792x336, and the portrait transposes (4:5 464x576, 3:4 448x600, 2:3 424x632, 9:16 384x688). 792x336 is the widest canvas there is; 704x304 is nearest 21:9 and fits. Anything over its ratio's pair is refused before the job is queued.

height.description: Canvas height. Max depends on aspect ratio.

no_background.description: Return subjects on a transparent background. Defaults True — pro is normally used for assets. Set False for scenes and backdrops.

reference_images.description: Up to 4 LABELLED reference images, as a JSON array. Each entry takes a "url" (preferred) OR a "base64": [{"url": "https://...", "usage": "character base"}, {"url": "https://...", "usage": "outfit and armour"}]. The "usage" note tells the model what to take from each image, which is what makes combining several references work. Prefer urls here especially — four inline images in one argument is four times the payload, and MCP clients truncate large arguments. Sizes are read from the images.

style_image_base64.description: One image whose art style (palette, outline, detail, shading) the result should match. Use style_copy to narrow which of those apply.

style_image_url.description: Alternative to style_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the style PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

style_copy.description: Which aspects to take from style_image_base64: any of color_palette, outline, detail, shading. Defaults to all four, or all but color_palette when a palette is given.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. The image is drawn for these colours and every pixel of the result is one of them.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8', 'NES'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours in each image (2-64), e.g. 6 for an NES-style sprite. With a palette, they are picked from it.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

get_image.name: get_image
get_image.description:
Get a raw-image result by job id, or a gallery image by `gallery:<id>`.

Returns the image(s) inline plus no-auth download URLs when completed, or
progress/error otherwise. A completed job also reports its gallery save:
the Creator ``asset_id`` once saved, or a failure note (the image is still
delivered) while the save is being retried.

job_id.description: The job id returned by any raw-image tool (create_image_pixflux, create_image_pixen, create_image_pro, edit_image, edit_image_pixen, transfer_outfit, inpaint_image, animate_image, image_to_pixelart, unzoom_image, correct_pixelart, reduce_colors, create_normal_map), or a gallery:<id> from list_images — images made on the website have no job id.

index.description: Return only this frame, inline. Use it to reach frames past the first few of a long animation without fetching a URL.

list_images.name: list_images
list_images.description:
List the images in your Creator gallery (pixellab.ai/create), newest first,
one line each: its `gallery:<id>` reference, description, size and frame
count. Pass the reference to get_image to download an image, to
pixelart_workbench to look at or edit it, and to save_to_asset to save a fix
over it.

limit.description: Maximum number of images to return

search.description: Filter by the description an image was made from, or its id, case-insensitive. 'knight' finds 'armored knight with a sword'.

edit_image.name: edit_image
edit_image.description:
Edit an existing image with a text instruction or a reference image (pro).

This returns YOUR image, edited — the pose, composition and pixel style are
preserved and only what you asked for changes. Use it to recolour armour, add
an accessory, change an expression, or restyle frames to match a reference.

Two modes, picked by what you pass:
- text edit: edit_image(images_base64=[<png>], description="give him a red cape")
- reference edit: edit_image(images_base64=[<png>], reference_image_base64=<png>)

Putting a reference outfit on an animation (2+ frames, motion kept)? Use
transfer_outfit — it is built for that. Reference mode here is for one image.

Related tools: create_image_pixflux(init_image_base64=...) regenerates the whole image
instead of editing it; create_map_object generates a NEW object matching a
map's style and returns a cutout, not your edited image.

Frame limit depends on output size: <=64px 16 frames, <=80px 9, <=128px 4,
larger 1 (one fewer in reference mode). Inputs max 512x512.

Cost: 10-25 generations (billed by the whole frame grid, so a single
64x64 edit costs the same as sixteen of them — batch your frames).
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to edit — pass a one-element list for a single image. Several frames get the SAME edit applied consistently (useful for animation frames or a character's directions). Max 512x512 each. PREFER image_urls — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s) to edit, in the same one-per-frame list form. PREFER THIS for anything but tiny sprites. Give urls OR base64, not both.

description.description: What to change (e.g. 'add a red wizard hat', 'make the armor gold'). Required unless reference_image_base64 is given.

reference_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to copy the appearance of (outfit/colors/details) onto the input image, keeping its pose. Switches the tool into reference mode; description then just refines the instruction. To put an outfit on ANIMATION frames, use transfer_outfit instead.

reference_image_url.description: Alternative to reference_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the reference PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

width.description: Output width. Defaults to the first input image's width.

height.description: Output height. Defaults to the first input image's height.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the inputs: if any frame has transparency they all stay transparent, otherwise they stay opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

edit_image_pixen.name: edit_image_pixen
edit_image_pixen.description:
Edit an image with a text instruction on the Pixen model (fast, 1 generation).

Returns YOUR image edited — pose, composition and pixel style are preserved
and only what you asked for changes.

Pick between the two edit tools:
- edit_image_pixen — this one; 1 generation, ~10-40s, ONE frame, input max
  256px per side and output max 256x256 in AREA. The default for a single
  sprite.
- edit_image — pro quality, 10-25 generations, ~30-90s, edits up to 16
  frames consistently in one call, accepts a reference image and inputs up
  to 512px. Worth it for animation frames, a character's directions, or when
  pixen's result isn't good enough.

Sizes: the input is capped PER SIDE at 256 (crop an oversized source —
never rescale pixel art); the output is capped by AREA at 256x256 =
65,536px, so 128x512 is fine but 320x320 is not. Output defaults to the
input's size. BOTH sides of both must be multiples of 4 — a 63x222 sprite
is rejected; pad it with transparent pixels to 64x224 first (padding keeps
the pixel grid, rescaling destroys it). Need a bigger canvas? edit_image
takes inputs up to 512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to change (e.g. 'give him a red cape', 'make the armor gold'). Same 1-500 bound the v2 endpoint enforces — an empty one would queue a job and spend a generation with nothing to edit towards.

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to edit. Max 256px per side, both sides multiples of 4 (pad with transparent pixels, never rescale). PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the PNG to edit. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

width.description: Output width, a multiple of 4. Output AREA must be at most 256x256 (65,536px), so 128x512 is fine but 320x320 is not. Defaults to the input image's width. The model re-renders at this size — it does not rescale.

height.description: Output height, a multiple of 4. Defaults to the input image's height.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the input: a transparent input stays transparent, an opaque one stays opaque.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

create_normal_map.name: create_normal_map
create_normal_map.description:
Make the normal map of a sprite or an animation, so a game engine can light it
(Pro 0.5 generation, Lite 0.1 generation).

The map is a PNG the sprite's size: RGB = which way each pixel faces (red right,
green up in the opengl convention, blue toward the viewer), alpha 255 wherever the
sprite shows and 0 elsewhere.
Each part of the sprite gets its own shape — a head is round, a hat a cone, a wall
faces south — so a light moving around it shades it the way a 3D model would.

An animation (`character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>`, a GIF, a strip) comes
back as a strip, one map per frame side by side in frame order, made from one
plan so the light stays steady as it moves.

Use it in Phaser with the Light2D pipeline:
  this.load.image('knight', ['knight.png', 'knight_n.png'])
  sprite.setPipeline('Light2D'); this.lights.enable().setAmbientColor(0x555555)
Godot: assign it as the sprite's normal map (CanvasTexture). Unreal: convention
"directx".

Each slider left out starts where the kind of picture puts it (an isometric box
gets flat faces), which suits most pictures. Lower
surface_detail for clean flat-shaded art, raise part_shapes for a rounder body;
strength makes the whole map stronger or flatter. Cracks, holes and gaps between
plates come out as grooves even when they glow.

mode="lite" (the default, recommended) reads the map from the art alone in about a
second and is almost always as good; mode="pro" plans every part (a head, an arm in
front of the body, a crack sunk in).

Sizes: each frame 8 to 512 px per side, up to 32 frames. Any colours (painted
art works); pixel art gives the cleanest parts.
Cost: Pro 0.5 generation, Lite 0.1 generation. Time: Pro ~15-60 s, Lite a few
seconds (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

image.description: The sprite: `character:<id>:<direction>` (a rotation), `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` (every frame of that animation), the same for `object:<id>`, `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>`, a pixelart_workbench result id, an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64. Prefer a reference or URL to inline base64.

convention.description: opengl: green = up (Godot, Unity, Phaser, most engines); directx: green = down (Unreal).

mode.description: lite (0.1 generation, recommended): from the art alone, in about a second, and almost always as good; set kind with it for isometric, sidescroller and UI art. pro (0.5 generation): each part of the picture is planned, its shape, what is in front, what is sunk into it.

kind.description: What the picture is: character (a character, creature or portrait), object (an item or effect), topdown (a map, scene or tileset seen from above), side (a side view: sidescroller tiles, a landscape), iso (isometric tiles and objects) or ui (panels, buttons, frames). Left out, it is read from the picture; set it when you know, above all for sidescroller, isometric and UI art.

strength.description: How far every pixel tilts away from facing the viewer.

outline_rounding.description: How much the outline rounds off: 0 keeps it flat to the edge.

part_shapes.description: How much the sprite's 3D parts (a round head, an arm's cylinder) add.

surface_detail.description: The art's own light and dark as bumps: chunks bulge, dark lines and cracks sink.

detail_softness.description: How much that detail is blurred, in px: low follows every pixel.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

transfer_outfit.name: transfer_outfit
transfer_outfit.description:
Reskin an existing animation with the outfit from a reference image (pro).

Every frame keeps its pose and motion; only the appearance changes to match
the reference — new armour on a walk cycle, a new colour scheme across an
attack, a weapon carried through the whole sequence.

transfer_outfit(frame_urls=[<f1>, <f2>, ...], reference_image_url=<outfit>)

The reference should be the SAME character in the new outfit. It does not
reliably turn one character into another.

Needs 2+ frames. For ONE image use edit_image(reference_image_base64=...)
instead; for a stored character's animation pass its frame URLs from
get_character.

Frame limit depends on output size (the reference takes one grid slot):
both sides 32-64px up to 15 frames, both 65-80px up to 8, larger side
81-256px up to 3. Frames over the limit: split across calls with the same
reference and seed.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from
Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: every pixel of
every frame is one of them (the palette, not the reference, sets the colours).

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: 10-25 generations, billed by the whole grid — 2 frames cost the same
as 15 at 64x64, so batch them. Generation time: ~1-2 minutes (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id); frames come back in input order.

frames_base64.description: Base64 PNG animation frames to reskin, in order (2 or more). Max 256x256 each. PREFER frame_urls — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

frame_urls.description: Alternative to frames_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the frame PNGs, in order. PREFER THIS for anything but tiny sprites. Give urls OR base64, not both.

reference_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG of the SAME character wearing the new outfit (e.g. a re-dressed or recoloured sprite of it). A different character as reference is unreliable — it can freeze the motion or barely change anything. Max 256x256.

reference_image_url.description: Alternative to reference_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the reference PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

additional_instructions.description: Optional guidance for the transfer, e.g. 'frames show the character from behind' or 'keep the sword in the right hand'.

width.description: Output frame width. Defaults to the widest frame. Frames and reference smaller than this are padded with transparency, centred — never scaled.

height.description: Output frame height. Defaults to the tallest frame.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the frames: if any frame has transparency the results are transparent, otherwise opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished frames are linked after generation.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

image_to_pixelart.name: image_to_pixelart
image_to_pixelart.description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art.

This is the general-purpose converter: give it any picture and get pixel art
back at the size you ask for. Use it when a user brings their own artwork,
a screenshot, or an AI render and wants it as a sprite.

Two dials decide how much licence the model takes:
- default (faithful=False, init_image_strength=0) — reinterprets the subject
  as pixel art. Cleanest sprites, least like the original.
- faithful=True with init_image_strength around 100-300 — reproduces the
  source. Use it when the user says "keep it exactly like this". Higher is
  NOT more faithful in a useful way: past ~300 the model stops transforming
  and returns the source image, which is not pixel art.

Related tools: create_portrait_character converts a picture into a character
portrait specifically; unzoom_image is what you want if the input is ALREADY
pixel art that has merely been upscaled — running it through here would
redraw art that only needed downscaling.

Input max area 2048x2048, output max 512x512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the image to convert. Any artwork, render or photo. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the source image. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

output_width.description: Width of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source width. Keep the source's aspect ratio.

output_height.description: Height of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source height.

faithful.description: Faithful mode. Stays true to the source instead of reinterpreting it as pixel art. Turn this on when the user wants THEIR artwork converted rather than a pixel-art take on it; pair it with a init_image_strength of 100-300.

init_image_strength.description: How strongly to start from the source image (img2img). 0 redraws from scratch using the source only as guidance; 100-300 keeps its composition and colors. Do NOT go higher to be 'more faithful' — past ~300 the model barely transforms the input and hands back the source rather than pixel art.

text_guidance_scale.description: How hard to push towards pixel-art style.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

image_to_pixelart_pro_flash.name: image_to_pixelart_pro_flash
image_to_pixelart_pro_flash.description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art with Pro Flash.

Redraws the picture as clean pixel art and picks the output size itself
(detected pixel scale), so there is no size parameter. Use image_to_pixelart
instead when the result must be an exact width and height. Optional
description steers the style (dithering, mood). For a console or palette look
(1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex
colours plus `palette_name`: the picture is drawn for them and every pixel of
the result is one of them.

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
Sources over 2048px on the longest side are scaled down first. Transparent
areas become a white background.

Cost: 6 generations. ~30-60 seconds. Returns one queued image; poll
get_image(job_id), then download.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

unzoom_image.name: unzoom_image
unzoom_image.description:
Downscale upscaled pixel art back onto its true pixel grid.

Pixel art found online is almost always scaled up — a 32x32 sprite saved at
512x512, where every art pixel is a 16x16 block. Every tool that takes a
reference or style image works far better on the real 32x32 sprite, and this
recovers it: the pixel grid is detected and the image is downsampled onto it.

Run this FIRST whenever a user supplies pixel art from outside PixelLab and
you are about to pass it to create_image_pixflux(init_image), a style image,
edit_image, or create_character. If the art was never upscaled it is already
at native size and this is unnecessary.

Do not confuse it with image_to_pixelart: that CONVERTS a non-pixel-art
picture, redrawing it. This one only downscales art that is already pixel art.

Input must be at least 256x256 (grid detection needs the pixels) and at most
2048x2048 in area.

The result is OPAQUE: grid detection works in RGB, so transparency in the
input is composited onto white first. If the user needs a cut-out sprite
back, tell them so rather than handing back a white-boxed result.

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in under a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the upscaled pixel art. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64, and unzoom inputs are big by definition.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the upscaled image. PREFER THIS. Give one, not both.

quantize.description: Palette handling for the result. 0 auto-detects a palette, -1 keeps every color the downsample produces, 2-256 quantizes to exactly that many colors.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

correct_pixelart.name: correct_pixelart
correct_pixelart.description:
Clean up pixel art — sharpen edges, drop stray pixels, tighten the palette.

Keeps the sprite on its existing pixel grid and at its existing size. Use it
on art that has been through a lossy pipeline, on hand-drawn art that needs
tidying, or on output from another tool that is nearly-but-not-quite on-grid.

Passing several frames in one call corrects them together, which is what you
want for an animation or a character's directions.

This does NOT resize. If each art pixel is a block of screen pixels the image
is upscaled, not damaged — run unzoom_image first, then correct if it still
needs it.

Transparency survives: the alpha channel is carried around the model and
re-applied, so a cutout sprite does not come back on a white box.

Max area 1024x1024 per frame.

Cost: 0.1 generations. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to clean up — pass a one-element list for a single image. All frames must be the same size. PREFER image_urls; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s), one per frame. PREFER THIS. Give urls OR base64, not both.

strength.description: How far the model may move from the art. 0.1 tidies stray pixels and edges; high values redraw more and can change details. Start low and only raise it if the art needs real repair.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

reduce_colors.name: reduce_colors
reduce_colors.description:
Quantize images onto a smaller, shared palette.

Pixel art reads as pixel art partly because of its restricted palette. AI
output and converted artwork often carry hundreds of near-identical colors;
this snaps them onto a tight palette, optionally with ordered dithering.

Passing several frames in one call is the point: they are quantized TOGETHER,
so an animation or a character's eight directions come back sharing ONE
palette instead of drifting apart frame by frame. Quantizing them one at a
time is the mistake this tool exists to prevent.

Three ways to choose the palette:
- omit num_colors and the palette image — the size is auto-detected
- num_colors — quantize to exactly this many colors
- palette_image — reuse the colors of an existing image (the game's palette)

The result carries a `palette` strip you can feed back as palette_image_base64
to lock later frames onto the same colors.

Total size limit across all frames is 512x512 worth of pixels (sixteen 64x64
frames, or four 128x128).

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in about a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to quantize — pass a one-element list for a single image. All frames must be the same size. PREFER image_urls; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s), one per frame. PREFER THIS. Give urls OR base64, not both.

num_colors.description: Target number of colors. Omit to auto-detect a good palette size from the images. Cannot be combined with a palette image.

palette_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG whose colors become the palette (max 256 colors) — use it to force frames onto an existing game palette. Cannot be combined with num_colors.

palette_image_url.description: Alternative to palette_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the palette image. Give one, not both.

dithering.description: Ordered dithering matrix size. Larger matrices give smoother gradients at the cost of a busier look.

dithering_strength.description: How strongly to dither. Ignored when dithering is 'none'.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

animate_image.name: animate_image
animate_image.description:
Animate any image from a text description of the motion.

Works on a loose sprite — unlike animate_character / animate_object, which
need an id of something PixelLab generated.

get_image returns frame_count + 1 images: index 0 is your input frame
unchanged, then the generated ones. Play them in order.

Examples:
- animate_image(first_frame_base64=<png>, action="walking forward", frame_count=8)
- pin the ending: animate_image(first_frame_base64=<open>, last_frame_base64=<closed>,
                                action="chest lid closing", frame_count=6)

Limits: frame max 256x256, and width x height x frame_count <= 524288 — so a
256x256 frame allows 8 frames, a 64x64 frame allows all 16.

Cost scales with total pixels (a 64x64 8-frame animation is 1 generation, a
128x128 16-frame one is 4). Generation time: ~30-180 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

action.description: The motion (e.g. 'walking forward', 'flame flickering', 'chest opening'). Describe movement, not appearance.

frame_count.description: Frames to generate — must be EVEN. 4 for idle loops, 8 for walk/run, 16 for complex actions. Large frames allow fewer frames.

first_frame_base64.description: Base64 PNG to animate — the first frame. Max 256x256. PREFER first_frame_url; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

first_frame_url.description: Alternative to first_frame_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the first frame PNG. PREFER THIS. Give one, not both.

last_frame_base64.description: Optional final frame, same size as the first, to pin where the motion ends (interpolation instead of open-ended animation).

last_frame_url.description: Alternative to last_frame_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the final frame PNG. Give one, not both.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the first frame: a transparent sprite animates on transparency, an opaque image stays opaque.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

animate_image_pixminimax.name: animate_image_pixminimax
animate_image_pixminimax.description:
Animate with text (PixMiniMax): animate any image from a motion description.

Works on a loose sprite — unlike animate_character / animate_object, which
need an id of something PixelLab generated. Same inputs as animate_image;
frame counts are multiples of four, capped by the frame's longer side (see Limits).

get_image returns frame_count + 1 images: index 0 is your input frame
unchanged, then the generated ones. Play them in order.

Examples:
- animate_image_pixminimax(first_frame_url=<png>, description="walking forward", frame_count=8)
- pin the ending: animate_image_pixminimax(first_frame_base64=<open>,
    last_frame_base64=<closed>, description="chest lid closing", frame_count=4)
- short prompt, expanded for you: animate_image_pixminimax(first_frame_url=<png>,
    description="shooting a bow", direction="south", enhance_prompt=True)

Caption fields (subject_description, initial_pose, view, direction) left out
are read off the image by an AI model, which can decline some requests; the
job then fails asking you to send them yourself.

Beta, every plan.
Limits: frame max 256x256; 4 to 40 frames in multiples of 4 at any size.

Cost: priced by generation time, which follows the UPSCALED canvas the model
works on — x4 up to 64px, x2 up to 128px, x1 above (longer side). So 64, 128
and 256 all price identically, and each is the MOST expensive size in its
neighbourhood. At 64/128/256: 4-8 frames = 1 generation, 12-16 = 2, 20-24 = 3,
28 = 4, 32-36 = 5, 40 = 6.
Four pixels over the step is ~3x cheaper on a long clip: 40 frames costs 6 at
128x128 and 2 at 132x132 (likewise 64x64 -> 68x68). Splitting helps too — four
8-frame calls cost 4 where one 32-frame call costs 5.
Generation time: ~1-6 minutes (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

Powered by MiniMax H3.

description.description: The motion (e.g. 'walking forward', 'flame flickering', 'chest opening'). Describe movement, not appearance.

frame_count.description: Frames to generate, a multiple of 4 from 4 to 40 at any size up to 256x256. 4 for idle loops, 8 for walk/run, 16+ for complex actions.

first_frame_base64.description: Base64 PNG to animate — the first frame. Max 256x256. PREFER first_frame_url; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

first_frame_url.description: Alternative to first_frame_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the first frame PNG. PREFER THIS. Give one, not both.

last_frame_base64.description: Optional final frame, same size as the first, to pin where the motion ends.

last_frame_url.description: Alternative to last_frame_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the final frame PNG. Give one, not both.

no_background.description: True (default) returns the frames on transparency; an opaque input is cut out of its first frame before animating. False keeps an opaque backdrop.

enhance_prompt.description: True rewrites a short description ('shooting a bow') as PixMiniMax's action caption before generating (+0.05 generations); the rewritten text is returned.

direction.description: Facing of the sprite (south = towards the camera), the model's facing caption field. Omit to have it read from the image.

view.description: Camera view of the sprite, the model's view caption field. Omit to have it read from the image.

subject_description.description: What the first frame shows, one noun phrase (e.g. 'a knight in silver plate armour'). Omit to have it read from the image.

initial_pose.description: The pose the first frame is in (e.g. 'standing upright with the sword lowered'). Omit to have it read from the image.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

animate_with_skeleton_v3.name: animate_with_skeleton_v3
animate_with_skeleton_v3.description:
Animate with skeleton v3 (beta): animate a sprite along a skeleton you pose, one per frame.

Every frame is drawn from the one reference image, so the character keeps its
identity while the pose is exactly what you send. Use this when you hold a rig
or can derive skeletons; for a stored PixelLab character, animate_character
with a template animation is far less work.
Nothing returns a template clip's keypoints to an API caller, so there is no
library of walk cycles to fetch: derive them from your sprite with `POST
/v2/estimate-skeleton`, bring your own rig (COCO-18 maps straight across, see
`keypoints`), or use animate_character(mode="skeleton-v3"), which poses a
template clip onto a stored character and needs no keypoints at all.

get_image returns exactly len(keypoints) images — the reference frame is not
echoed back. Play them in order.

Limits: sprite max {MAX_DIMENSION}x{MAX_DIMENSION}; {MIN_FRAMES} to {MAX_FRAMES}
frames, each skeleton holding all 18 humanoid joints.

Cost: priced by generation time, which barely moves with length, so every
legal frame count falls in one of three steps — 3 frames = 2 generations,
4 to 14 = 3, 15 = 4.
Generation time: ~3-6 minutes (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What the character LOOKS like, as a noun phrase: 'blonde vampire with a red cape'. Colours, clothing, held items — not the motion, which the skeletons carry.

direction.description: Facing of the sprite (south = towards the camera).

keypoints.description: The motion: one skeleton per frame you get back, 3-15 frames. Each is a list of all 18 joints, {"label": "RIGHT KNEE", "x": 0.52, "y": 0.71, "z_index": 9}, with x/y as fractions 0-1 of the image. The 18 labels, exactly (every one required once per frame, order does not matter): NOSE, NECK, RIGHT SHOULDER, RIGHT ELBOW, RIGHT ARM, LEFT SHOULDER, LEFT ELBOW, LEFT ARM, RIGHT HIP, RIGHT KNEE, RIGHT LEG, LEFT HIP, LEFT KNEE, LEFT LEG, RIGHT EYE, LEFT EYE, RIGHT EAR, LEFT EAR. That set and order are OpenPose COCO-18, so `ARM` is the WRIST and `LEG` is the ANKLE (shoulder -> elbow -> ARM, hip -> knee -> LEG) and a COCO-18 pose from an external tool maps across 1:1. LEFT/RIGHT are the character's own sides, not the viewer's: facing `east` the RIGHT limbs are the near ones, mirrored for `west`, near-equal for `south`/`north`. `z_index` is a draw order — any int, default 0; no template prescribes values for it, it is yours. `depth` is optional (0-255, ~128 = the body's centre, higher = nearer the camera); left out, it is taken from the template body for this direction — which is the easier path, since that is where near/far already comes from (a mannequin at side/east runs RIGHT ARM 156 against LEFT ARM 100).

first_frame_keypoints.description: The skeleton of the pose first_frame is already IN, same 18 joints and labels as `keypoints`. The model redraws that frame first and learns the background key and the colours from the redraw, so a skeleton that does not match the image quietly costs transparency and colour accuracy. This frame is not returned. To get these for your own sprite, call `POST /v2/estimate-skeleton` (POST, not GET). There is no MCP tool for it, but it needs no new credential: MCP and v2 authenticate the same token, so the one already in your MCP client config works verbatim — send it as `Authorization: Bearer <that token>` with a body of `{"image": {"type": "base64", "base64": "<png>"}}` — no other fields are accepted. It answers `{"keypoints": [{"label": ..., "x": ..., "y": ..., "z_index": ...}]}`, and x/y come back as fractions 0-1 of YOUR original image, so they drop straight in here. ANY size works: it pads to the nearest of 16/32/64/128/256 internally and converts the coordinates back, so a 40x40 or 56x56 sprite needs no padding from you. 0.1 generations per call. A fully transparent frame is refused with 422 before anything is charged.

first_frame_base64.description: Base64 PNG of the sprite to animate. Max 256x256. PREFER first_frame_url; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

first_frame_url.description: Alternative to first_frame_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the sprite PNG. PREFER THIS. Give one, not both.

template_id.description: The body a joint's missing `depth` is taken from. A quadruped posed with mannequin depth comes out flat.

view.description: Camera angle the sprite is drawn at. Must match the sprite, or the motion is posed for a different camera.

no_background.description: True (default) returns the frames on transparency.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

pixelart_workbench.name: pixelart_workbench
pixelart_workbench.description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Commands: check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,…] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side
Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise
Sheets and frames (returns a NEW image id):
- split <image> --grid 3x3 — a sprite sheet, strip or grid as an animation,
  one frame per cell (columns x rows)
- join <image> <image> … [--as sheet|rows|animation] [--columns n] — pictures
  or animations as one sprite sheet, one per row, or one animation
- scale <image> --by 4 — the same picture or animation bigger, each pixel a
  4x4 block (a sticker, a print); nothing is redrawn
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`. Anything unclear: `describe cli`,
`describe lint_rules`, `describe ramps`. Free for subscribers.

argv.description: One command line, e.g. 'lint <drawing_id> --rules outline_gap' or ['edit', '<id>', '--changes', '[…]']. Omit it for the playbook. A subject is an id or an image reference (`character:<id>:south`, a data URL, an https link) — never a file path; the server writes the output and returns a new id. Start with 'describe cli' for the full command list.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

vfx_workbench.name: vfx_workbench
vfx_workbench.description:
Make an animated pixel-art effect (spell, hit, explosion, aura, projectile,
weather...) yourself, around the user's sprite or on its own: drop in tuned
parts, write layers, look at every render, then export. Export saves it to the
user's My effects on pixellab.ai (re-editable there with sliders) and returns a
GIF and a spritesheet PNG + JSON; --game-pack adds a ZIP of every piece for a game
engine (--part <id> just one). Free for subscribers.

Commands:
- start [--sprite <image>] [--projectile <image>] [--preset <name>] -> step id
- <step id> <tool> '<JSON>' -> add_part, set_part, remove_part, throw, render,
  get_preset, get_part, list_parts; a change returns a new step id
- <step id> export [--name N] [--replace <effect id>] [--game-pack | --part <id>]
- describe start | parts | recipe | craft | cookbook | edits | presets | tools
Sprites and exports are pixelart_workbench ids, so the two work together.
Start with describe start.

argv.description: One command, e.g. ['start', '--sprite', 'character:<id>:south'], ['<step id>', 'add_part', '{"name": "fire_burst"}'] or ['<step id>', 'export', '--name', 'Fireball']. Omit it for the guide.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

save_to_asset.name: save_to_asset
save_to_asset.description:
Save pixel art into one of your characters, objects, Creator gallery
images or tilesets, replacing a rotation, one direction of an animation, a
gallery image or a tileset's tiles — or add it to the gallery as a new image
(free, no generation).

Use it to keep a fix made with pixelart_workbench or another image tool: the
character and object creators, the Creator gallery, the map editor, downloads
and game projects then show the new pixels. The image must match what it replaces —
the same canvas size and the same number of frames; a different size can go
to the gallery as a new image. Save each direction with its own call. The
replaced frames are kept: the reply gives the save_to_asset call that puts
them back.

Examples:
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:south")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:east:<group id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="object:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:new",
  description="knight holding a sword, idle")
- save_to_asset(image="<edited sheet>", target="tileset:<id>")

image.description: What to save: a pixelart_workbench result id (`<id>`, or `<id>:<view>` for a drawing), `job:<id>` / `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>` (an image POSTed to /v2/uploads), an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64.

target.description: Where to save it. A rotation: `character:<id>:<direction>`, `object:<id>:<direction>`, or `object:<id>` for a one-direction object. One direction of an animation: the same with `:<group id>` added (get_character / get_object show each animation's [group: …] id). A Creator gallery image: `gallery:<id>` to replace it (list_images shows each image's reference), `gallery:new` to add the image as a new one. A top-down or sidescroller tileset: `tileset:<id>` with its whole sheet (the download_png layout, same size), keeping its id and tile layout.

description.description: Only with target="gallery:new": what the image shows, kept as its gallery description so the website and list_images(search=...) can find it.

create_map.name: create_map
create_map.description:
Create an empty map seeded with a tileset and everything connected to it,
or with a tile group.

The map starts with no painted cells — paint it with edit_map, which grows
the bounds as you go. Tile size comes from the seed tileset. A map started
from a tile group is a tile map instead: its tiles go on tile layers with
place_map_tiles, which can stack them.

Being in the same family makes a terrain AVAILABLE, not blendable: only a
pair with its own tileset renders a border. Check with view_map, which names
every unpaired pair and the create_topdown_tileset call that joins it.

tileset_id.description: Tileset to seed the map from (from list_topdown_tilesets). Every tileset connected to it — same tile size, sharing a base tile id — is attached too, so their terrains are available to paint. A pair still needs its OWN tileset to blend: two terrains from the family with none between them meet with a hard edge (a straight seam), and view_map names any such pair with the call that blends it.

tile_group_id.description: Instead of tileset_id: a tile group (from list_tiles_pro — isometric, hex, oblique or square tiles, or a building kit) to start a tile map from. Place and stack its tiles with place_map_tiles; add more groups there with add_group.

project_id.description: Attach the map to this game project. Without it the map exists but never syncs into a project workspace, so a game cannot load it.

delete_map.name: delete_map
delete_map.description:
Delete one of your maps. Immediate — there is no undo.

A map wired into a project is loaded by that project's game by id, so
deleting one that a game still references breaks that game's next build.
The response says how many projects referenced it.

map_id.description: The map to delete, from list_maps

list_maps.name: list_maps
list_maps.description:
List your maps, most recently edited first.

Pass `search` to find one by name — accounts reach four figures of maps, so
paging is not a way to look something up. Maps are made in PixelLab's Map
Workshop; use get_map to see one and edit_map to paint terrain on it.

search.description: Only maps whose name contains this (case-insensitive)

offset.description: Skip this many, to page deeper

get_map.name: get_map
get_map.description:
Show a map as an ASCII grid, one character per terrain cell.

With no crop you get the whole map downsampled to fit; pass x/y/width/height
for a 1:1 view of one area. Coordinates are terrain cells and can be
negative — the rulers show the real numbers, so read them off the view and
pass them straight to edit_map.

Maps built from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique and similar tiles) show
their tile layers: for every cell the tile on top and the stack level it
sits on, plus each stacked column spelled out. Change those with
place_map_tiles.

x.description: Crop: left edge, in terrain cells (q on tile layers)

y.description: Crop: top edge, in terrain cells (r on tile layers)

edit_map.name: edit_map
edit_map.description:
Paint terrain on a map: rivers and roads with `path`, areas with `rect`.

You choose regions, not tiles — the tileset picks the actual tile art for
every corner, and shoreline rows between terrains are inserted for you. Name
a terrain the map doesn't have yet and the tileset providing it is attached
automatically, along with any tileset connected to it. A tileset not
connected to this map attaches only when you name its terrain exactly; it
meets the map with hard edges (straight seams) until a tileset joins them.

Returns what changed, an ASCII view of the affected area, and — when the edit
used new art or went wrong — a rendered image of it. Pass show=true to see
the image any time; use view_map to look at somewhere you did not just paint.

oneOf.description: A stroke through waypoints — rivers, roads, coastlines.
An axis-aligned area — fields, plazas, blocks of ground.

dry_run.description: Preview the result and warnings without saving

show.description: Also return a rendered IMAGE of the edited area. On by default whenever the edit brings in a terrain you have not seen rendered, or leaves tiles no tileset can draw.

view_map.name: view_map
view_map.description:
Render the map to an image and return it, terrain and objects together.

Use this to judge how a map LOOKS — get_map's ASCII shows you where terrain
is, never what it looks like. Crop with x/y/width/height (the same cell
coordinates get_map and edit_map use) to inspect an area closely.

This renders from the terrain grid, so it always shows the map's CURRENT
state, including edits a human has not opened Map Workshop to see.

x.description: Crop: left edge, in terrain cells

y.description: Crop: top edge, in terrain cells

place_map_object.name: place_map_object
place_map_object.description:
Place objects or characters on a map, at a terrain cell or an exact pixel.

Objects are how a map gets trees, houses, rocks and NPCs — terrain painting
(edit_map) only covers ground. A tileset tiles a SURFACE, so anything with a
silhouette has to be an object.

Position: x/y stands the sprite on that cell (the coordinates get_map
shows). world_x/world_y puts it at an exact world pixel instead, as Map
Workshop's free drag does — use it to match positions from a game scene or
an isometric layout that does not fall on the cell grid.

For many objects pass `placements`: one call, one save.

Returns a picture of the result by default, because a placement that is one
cell off, or far bigger than you expected, is invisible in text.

x.description: Terrain cell to stand the object on, as in get_map

y.description: Terrain cell to stand the object on, as in get_map

world_x.description: Exact position in world pixels, instead of x/y — the space of the map's object boundingBox and the game's sprites

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (default) = the sprite's bottom-centre; 'top_left' = the box origin, box_px in list_map_objects

direction.description: Facing for a character (south, north, east...). Leave unset for objects — most have a single sprite and it is picked automatically.

layer.description: Draw order; higher is on top. Defaults to the next layer.

placements.description: Place many in one call, instead of the single-placement arguments: [{"object_id":"…","x":3,"y":4}, {"object_id":"…","world_x":412,"world_y":230,"anchor":"foot"}, {"character_id":"…","x":1,"y":1,"direction":"south"}]. Each item takes the same fields as above. One save for all; if any item is invalid nothing is placed.

x.description: Terrain cell to stand it on

y.description: Terrain cell to stand it on

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (bottom-centre, default) or 'top_left' (the stored box origin, box_px in list_map_objects)

layer.description: Draw order; higher is on top

show.description: Return a rendered image of the placement

place_map_tiles.name: place_map_tiles
place_map_tiles.description:
Place, stack and erase tiles on a map's tile layers — the map editor's tile
painting, with its Stack layer control.

A map made from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique, square tiles) keeps
each group as a tile layer; get_map lists them and shows, per cell, the
tile on top and its stack level. A cell holds a column of tiles: level 0
is the ground, and each level above sits one tile height higher, so a
`stack` of 3 builds a pillar and "on_top" builds on whatever is there.

Placing on a cell's level replaces the tile already there. As in the
editor, a tile placed on one ground layer clears that same cell and level
on any other ground layer drawn on the same grid.

Tiles go down exactly as given: for connected sets, pick the tile drawn
for that spot's neighbours (get_tiles_pro lists each tile's mask).

A building kit is several layers: floor, interior walls, outer walls, roof
(when the kit has roof pieces) and pieces (pillars, doorways, stairs). Lay
floor tiles and the outer walls follow the floor's outline. Interior walls
and roofs take no tile: each cell's piece follows its neighbours. A doorway
is cut into the wall at that cell, and stairs lay both halves. get_map lists
what each kit layer takes.

Returns what changed and a view of the area: the top tile and the top
level of every cell, and each stacked column level by level.

oneOf.description: Put one tile on cells, `stack` levels high.

layer.description: Tile layer index, as listed by get_map

area.description: An inclusive block of cells: q..q+width-1, r..r+height-1.

tile.description: Tile index in the layer's tile group. Left out on a building kit's interior-wall and roof layers, whose pieces follow their neighbours

oneOf.description: Remove tiles: everything from `level` up, or the top `stack` with on_top.

layer.description: Tile layer index, as listed by get_map

area.description: An inclusive block of cells: q..q+width-1, r..r+height-1.

oneOf.description: Lay another tile group on the map as new layers, after the existing ones.

list_map_objects.name: list_map_objects
list_map_objects.description:
List the objects and characters placed on a map, with their cell positions.

Gives you the placement id that move_map_object and remove_map_object take.
A placement id is per-PLACEMENT, not per-asset — the same tree placed twice
has two ids.

move_map_object.name: move_map_object
move_map_object.description:
Move a placed object or character to a different cell or an exact pixel, or
change its layer.

Keeps its sprite and refs. world_x/world_y positions it to the pixel, as Map
Workshop's free drag does; `layer` alone re-orders it without moving it.

x.description: Cell to stand it on, as in get_map

y.description: Cell to stand it on, as in get_map

world_x.description: Exact position in world pixels, instead of x/y

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (default) = the sprite's bottom-centre; 'top_left' = the box origin, box_px in list_map_objects

layer.description: New draw order (higher is on top). Pass it alone to change only the layer: the stored position, fractions included, is untouched.

show.description: Return a rendered image of the result

remove_map_object.name: remove_map_object
remove_map_object.description:
Remove placed objects or characters from a map.

Deletes placements only — the object or character itself is untouched and can
be placed again. Pass `placement_id` for one, or `asset_id` to clear every
placement of one asset at once.

asset_id.description: Remove EVERY placement of this object or character instead — the asset_id column in list_map_objects. Use it to clear one prop from a whole map in a single call.

sandbox_create_session.name: sandbox_create_session
sandbox_create_session.description: Create a sandbox session for a game project. Returns session_id + file tree + git log. Working directory: /workspace. Tools: Node.js 20, npm, git, tsc. Session expires after 30 min idle.

list_projects.name: list_projects
list_projects.description: List your game projects with IDs, branches, and git clone URLs.

sandbox_destroy_session.name: sandbox_destroy_session
sandbox_destroy_session.description: Destroy a sandbox session. Syncs to storage by default.

sandbox_bash.name: sandbox_bash
sandbox_bash.description: Run a shell command in the sandbox (/workspace). Available: node, npm, git, tsc, and `wrangler deploy` — builds + deploys the game's unified Cloudflare Worker (frontend + /api + multiplayer /room -> {slug}.pixellab.run) and runs a smoke test. Use `wrangler deploy` to deploy (there is no separate deploy tool); `wrangler tail` shows the worker's runtime logs. Don't run build.sh / npm build directly — wrangler deploy builds.

sandbox_run.name: sandbox_run
sandbox_run.description:
Code Mode: run a JavaScript snippet in the project sandbox (Node, cwd /workspace) to do many file/shell ops in ONE call instead of chaining sandbox_read/write/edit/bash. Your code is an async function body with a typed `sandbox` API + console.log:
  sandbox.read(path)->string · sandbox.write(path,content) · sandbox.edit(path,old,new) (errors if old not found) · sandbox.ls(dir?)->string[] · sandbox.sh(cmd)->stdout
`return` a value to report it. Example: `const p=JSON.parse(sandbox.read('website/package.json')); console.log(p.name); return sandbox.ls('website/src');`  Returns console output + the returned value (or the error). Use `sandbox.sh('wrangler deploy')` to deploy.

sandbox_read.name: sandbox_read
sandbox_read.description: Read a file from the sandbox. Returns content with line numbers.

sandbox_write.name: sandbox_write
sandbox_write.description: Create or overwrite a file in the sandbox. Creates parent directories automatically.

sandbox_edit.name: sandbox_edit
sandbox_edit.description: Edit a file via search-and-replace. old_string must match exactly once.

sandbox_sync.name: sandbox_sync
sandbox_sync.description: Save current git state to persistent storage.

sandbox_deploy_worker.name: sandbox_deploy_worker
sandbox_deploy_worker.description: Build and deploy a Cloudflare Worker for a chat project. Deploys the unified Worker (frontend + /api + multiplayer /room) to {project_slug}.pixellab.run. Requires an active sandbox session.

sandbox_undeploy.name: sandbox_undeploy
sandbox_undeploy.description: Remove deployed files from S3 and invalidate CloudFront cache for a project branch. Use after deleting a project or to clean up a stale preview deployment.

sandbox_playtest.name: sandbox_playtest
sandbox_playtest.description: Playtest a deployed game using a vision AI subagent. The subagent opens the game in a browser, takes screenshots, and interacts via keyboard/mouse following your instruction. Returns a text report of observations. Takes 30-60s. Cost: ~1 generation, usually less.

sandbox_read_image.name: sandbox_read_image
sandbox_read_image.description: Read an image file from the sandbox and analyze it with a vision model. Returns a text description of the image contents. Cost: ~1 generation, usually less.

path.description: Path to the image file in the sandbox (e.g. 'game/assets/player.png').

question.description: What to analyze about the image — be specific (e.g. 'Is the player sprite facing south?', 'What colors are used in this tileset?').

chat_list_conversations.name: chat_list_conversations
chat_list_conversations.description: List your chat conversations. Excludes branches. Shows processing status.

project_id.description: Filter by project ID

chat_get_messages.name: chat_get_messages
chat_get_messages.description: Get messages from a conversation. Strips HTML from assistant responses.

chat_send_message.name: chat_send_message
chat_send_message.description: Send a message to a chat conversation and wait for the agent response. Creates a new conversation if conversation_id is not provided. The agent runs in background (building games, creating assets, etc). Polls until the agent finishes, then returns the assistant's reply. Typical response time: 30s-5min depending on task complexity. Cost: the agent's model usage, billed like a /chat message on the website; the reply states what the turn cost.

content.description: Message to send to the agent

conversation_id.description: Conversation ID. Omit to create a new conversation.

project_id.description: Project ID (used when creating a new conversation)

agent_list.name: agent_list
agent_list.description:
List the deployed AI agents you own (the 'deploy your own agent' projects). Returns each
agent's slug — pass it as `agent` to agent_inspect / agent_talk.

agent_inspect.name: agent_inspect
agent_inspect.description:
Debug a deployed agent's LIVE runtime: its state, recent chat, LLM/tool traces (errors first,
with the model's real input/output), and grown memory (journal/agenda/lessons/feedback). Use this
to see what the agent ACTUALLY did before changing its source. `focus='traces'` zooms in on bad turns.

agent.description: Agent slug (omit if you only have one)

agent_talk.name: agent_talk
agent_talk.description:
Send a message to a deployed agent (as its owner) and get its reply — to test how it responds
while you're working on it. Goes through the agent's normal chat loop (so it may run its tools).

message.description: What to say to the agent

agent.description: Agent slug (omit if you only have one)

get_balance.name: get_balance
get_balance.description: Check your account balance: remaining credits (USD) and subscription generations.

get_upload_url.name: get_upload_url
get_upload_url.description:
Get a URL to upload a local image file to, without needing your API token.

Use it whenever you have an image on disk and a tool wants an image: send
the file with one curl, and pass the `upload:<id>` it returns to any
parameter that takes an image URL (image_urls, reference_image_url,
init_image_url, a style_image "url" ...). This avoids pasting base64 into a
tool call, which clients truncate and can corrupt. Free.

The URL works for 15 minutes and for any number of files. Uploads are kept
3 days. An animated GIF keeps all its frames.

search_knowledge.name: search_knowledge
search_knowledge.description:
Search the Phaser/game dev knowledge base for tips, patterns, and code examples.

Returns semantically matched tips from the curated knowledge base — useful
for Phaser 4 patterns, TypeScript game dev, Vite build issues, map systems,
collision, camera follow, and other game builder topics.

query.description: Search query — describe the Phaser/TypeScript/game dev topic you need help with (e.g. 'camera follow player', 'collision detection', 'map transitions').

cancel_job.name: cancel_job
cancel_job.description:
Cancel a pending or processing background job.

Releases the concurrency slot immediately so you can start new work.
Already-completed or already-failed jobs are left unchanged.

list_jobs.name: list_jobs
list_jobs.description:
List your active background jobs (pending + processing).

Use this to find stuck jobs you can cancel with cancel_job.

include_recent.description: Include recently completed/failed jobs (last 30 min). Default: only active jobs.

wait_for_jobs.name: wait_for_jobs
wait_for_jobs.description:
Wait for your running generations instead of sleeping and polling.

Returns as soon as min_finished (default 1) of your pending/processing jobs
finish, immediately when none are running, or at the timeout. Free. Then call
the matching get_* tool for the result; call wait_for_jobs again for the jobs
still running.

timeout_seconds.description: Give up waiting after this many seconds (jobs keep running). If your client times out the call itself (some stop a tool at ~60s), pass a value under that limit and call again.

min_finished.description: Return once this many of your running jobs have finished (or all of them, if fewer are running). 1 frees you to fill a slot the moment one opens; raise it for a large batch so one call covers several.
